en: Private Notes on the *Brahmajāla-sūtra Bodhisattva Precept Text*, Scroll One, composed by Master Xiao.
In order to explain this sūtra, I shall briefly distinguish two sections: first, the explanation of the title; second, the entry into the text.
Explanation: First, regarding the interpretation of the title: what is called the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Bodhisattva Precept Text) is a designation established through a metaphor of the Dharma;
therefore, it is not the actual title of this scripture. If one were to state the actual title of this scripture, it should be called the *Brahmajāla-sūtra Bodhisattva Mind-Ground*.
Regarding the title "Brahmajāla" (The Brahma’s Net): it is named according to a metaphor.

This is because when the Tathāgata preached this Dharma, he observed that the Brahmā Heaven was covered by a jeweled net over its banners; since he spoke [the name] based on this observation, this sutra is called the *Brahmajāla*.
There are sutras named solely after the Dharma, such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and others; there are also sutras named solely after a person.

Regarding titles: there are those such as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, which take the name of the scripture itself as the title; or those such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which employ both the Dharma and a metaphor as the title.
As for this present scripture, it uses a metaphor alone as its title. It employs the metaphor of a net to represent the Dharma taught by the Buddha, which briefly has three meanings.
First, the Tathāgata is able to expound the Dharma-gates of immeasurable oceans of worlds; this refers to the lotus.
The World upon the Flower. As for this world, from the level wind-circle below up to the Supreme Treasury wind-circle, there are immeasurable worlds;
there are also immeasurable worlds extending horizontally throughout the ten directions, as explained at length in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Regarding such worlds, those worlds are not this world, and this world is also not those worlds.
Regarding those worlds: if these worlds were distinct and not devoid of meaning, then they would correspond to the mesh of a net;
this mesh would not be that mesh, and that mesh would not be this mesh.

Furthermore, although worlds may be distinct and infinite, if they are subsumed within the pure land of the *dharmatā*, there is no world that is not the pure land of *dharmatā*. This principle corresponds to the mesh.
Although they are not without distinction, that which is designated as "the net" does not fail to encompass the meaning of "the eye.

Therefore, the net is used as a metaphor for the Dharma taught by the Buddha. Second, regarding the discussion of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): this dharma is not that dharma, and that dharma is not this dharma;
yet, through their differentiation, the myriad distinctions are established. This principle corresponds to the statement here: "the eye is not that."
The eye: that eye does not possess the meaning of being a "mere" eye. Furthermore, the single flavor of true emptiness is taken as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Although the distinctions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are not non-existent, when one subsumes conventional phenomena under the ultimate, every single phenomenon is nothing other than the One Suchness (*tathatā*).
This principle corresponds to using the net to subsume the eyes; the eyes are nothing other than the net. Therefore, the metaphor of the net is used to represent the sutra-eyes.
Furthermore, thirdly, regarding the Dharma-gates taught by the Buddha: although there are many such gates, they do not transcend the two gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).
This is because they are able to harmonize all phenomena, and their essence is the single Suchness of the Dharma-realm; therefore, they are called *śamatha*.

Although one realizes that all phenomena are nothing other than this single Suchness, one is still able to illuminate the conventionally existent phenomena as being not without principle; therefore, it is called *vipaśyanā*. For what reason is this said?

Regarding the "numerous dharma-gates": there are those who enter the Path through specific contemplation (*pṛthag-darśana*), and there are those who enter the Path through general contemplation (*sāmānya-darśana*).

If one considers these in terms of the contemplation of the Path, although they do not go beyond the two gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight), they are nonetheless established as distinct names.
In order to cause others to enter and observe the distinct [teachings], many [methods] are taught. Although there are many doors, they nonetheless lead to the principle which is non-dual.
It is like a city that has four gates; although the gates through which one enters are not the same, the entry into the city itself is non-dual.
This meaning is likewise so. If one considers them according to their distinct doors, although this door is not that door and that door is not this door, yet if one...
Regarding the general gate encompassing the specific gates: there is nothing that is not subsumed within the two gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight);
thus, all things are subsumed within *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Although there are distinctions among the "eyes," the "net" encompasses the eyes; there is no eye that is not part of the net.

Because these three meanings taught by the Tathāgata correspond to this principle of the net and the eyes, and because the title is derived from this metaphor, it is called the *Brahmajāla* (Net of Brahma). This refers to this particular section.
Regarding the specific names: this is a general title for the sutra, and the general title of the sutra is as commonly explained.
As for the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind": *Bodhisattva*—in its full Sanskrit phonetics—should be called *bodhisattvamahāsattva*.
*Bodhi* is named the mind of the Way (*mārgacitta*); *sattva* is named sentient beings (*sattva*); and *mahāsattva* is named the one who possesses the great mind of the Way (*mahāmārgacitta*).
"Sentient beings" (*sattva*). A *bodhisattva* refers to one who practices for their own benefit; a *mahāsattva* refers to one who practices for the benefit of others.
Since the practice of benefiting others is superior to that of benefiting oneself, they are called "beings with the mind of the Great Way.
This unsurpassed bodhicitta is the fruit, while "sentient beings" is the cause. Because cause and fruit are combined into a single name, it is called the "mind of the Great Way."

It is for all sentient beings. Regarding the "ground of the mind" (*cittabhūmi*): it has the meaning of "that which can produce" and the meaning of "that upon which one dwells. This is the meaning of "ground. Briefly, there are three explanations of this meaning of "ground.
First, it is said that the forty minds prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) and the ten minds on the grounds—these fifty minds in total—are the "grounds" where practicing Bodhisattvas dwell;
therefore, they constitute the "ground of the mind. Dwelling within these fifty grounds, one is able to abide in *bodhi*.
Regarding the mind: one interpretation states that the threefold aggregate of precepts (tri-skandhaka-śīla) serves as the ground of abiding, while the bodhicitta serves as that which abides.
Another interpretation states that the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) serves as the ground of abiding, while the practitioner serves as that which abides.

Although all sentient beings transmigrate through the five destinies, none ever depart from outside the single dharma-realm; they are all the dharma-realm itself, serving both as the ground of abiding and as that which abides.
"Those" refers to the minds of sentient beings. "Chapter" (*pin*) is as commonly explained. This present fascicle is one chapter within the large section of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
The upper fascicle clarifies the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground; this lower fascicle clarifies the characteristics of the Bodhisattva precepts.
Regarding that large section, it consists of one hundred and twelve fascicles and sixty-one chapters. This particular chapter is the [first]...
This is the "Chapter on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground. The Honored Teacher said: "If one were to discuss the title of this sutra in full detail, it should be stated as:
*The Brahmajāla Sūtra: The Dharma-Door of the Mind-Ground Spoken by Vairocana Buddha; the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Precepts Spoken by Śākyamuni Buddha*.
However, for the sake of brevity, it is not necessary to include all of this here. Having thus concluded the explanation of the title.
Second, regarding the textual analysis and explanation: this present sutra is a single chapter within the section of the formal exposition (*samyag-deśanā*) among many sections;

therefore, it lacks a separate threefold division of introduction, formal exposition, and dissemination (*nidāna*, *deśanā*, *parīndanā*). Nevertheless, according to the meaning and the structural arrangement of the text, it is not without these three divisions.

From the passage beginning with "Now I, Vairocana... down to "the first purity," the text constitutes the introductory section (*upodghāta*). From [the passage] beginning with "The Buddha... [down to the end of the chapter], the formal exposition is established. *Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment. The translation reflects the available portion.*
From "Having addressed all the sons of the Buddha" onwards, up to "the present bodhisattvas now recite," this section corresponds to the formal exposition (*bhāṣya*).

From "Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively" onwards, up to the end of the scroll, the words should be diligently upheld. Within the initial introductory section (*nidāna*), there are also three parts.
The three lines and three phrases of verse beginning with "I, now Vairocana... constitute the introduction by Vairocana Buddha.
The passage beginning with "At that time, the hundreds of thousands of millions" and ending with the seven lines and three phrases is the introduction to Śākyamuni of other lands.
The passage beginning with "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha" and continuing as prose is the introduction to Śākyamuni of this land.

Within the initial introduction to Vairocana Buddha, there are also two sections: the first uses two lines to manifest the principal teacher of transformation; the second, beginning with "Pervading everywhere," consists of two lines.
Regarding the verse, the first three lines—"A multitude listening to the Dharma have all come to where I am"—enumerate the assembly of listeners.
Within the first two lines, there are also two parts: the upper line correctly identifies the person, while the lower line clarifies the dwelling place.
Regarding the initial statement, "I, now": this Vairocana Buddha is called "I" because he has already attained both the provisional and the real self (*ātman*).

While those of the Two Vehicles have departed from the divine self (*puruṣa-ātman*) of the non-Buddhists and thus attain a provisional self, they remain attached to non-self (*anātman*) and do not attain the true self.
The Tathāgata, being able to depart from both the divine self of the non-Buddhists and the attachment to non-self of the Two Vehicles, fully possesses both types of self.
Furthermore, because one is able to be free from the two selves of person and phenomena, one attains the non-self of non-self and the self of sovereign mastery;

it is not a self characterized by the pride of "I" as discussed in worldly treatises. As for Vairocana, the translated name is "Perfectly Pure," meaning that there is no defiled dharma that has not been exhausted.

Therefore, one is able to manifest pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) without anything being unattained; for this reason, it is called "perfect purity" (*pariśuddha*). *Vairocana* translates as "vast perfect purity.

As for "vast" (*viśāla*), it means there is nothing it does not penetrate throughout the dharma-realm of the ten directions, and nothing it does not pervade from the limits of the three periods of time;
hence it is called "vast perfect purity. Regarding the manifestation of names: the name Śākya is manifested within the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), while [the name] Virocana...
Rocana is manifested from the *saṃbhogakāya*; Vairocana arises from within the *dharmakāya*.
If one takes the names as the essence [of the bodies], each individual name universally designates the three bodies. This is known to be so because the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"In these four continents, the names of the Buddhas differ; some are called Siddhārtha, some are called Śākyamuni, and some are called Rocana."
That number is ten thousand; thus we know it refers to the universal [manifestation]. How is this known? Because Vairocana is designated as the common name for the three bodies (*trikāya*).
Within this single Buddha-gate of the sutra, since it says, "I am now Vairocana," we know it is a universal name.
Why is this Vairocana Buddha endowed with the three bodies, and why do the hundreds of millions of Śākyamunis proceed [there]?

Because they see [the Buddha], we know that the Dharmakāya Buddha is also received by the thousand Śākyamunis of the Nirmāṇakāya; thus, the assembly of Bodhisattvas on the stages (bhūmi) are all able to see him.
Because they see [him], we know that the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha is received by the hundred billion emanations of Śākyamuni;
thus, the assembly prior to the stages (pūrvabhūmika) go to see him. Although he thus possesses the meaning of the three bodies, he is collectively named "I am now the Lu... [Avalokiteśvara].
Vairocana is a Buddha within this single Buddha-gate and thus possesses the meaning of the three bodies (trikāya).

This is because, within the mental continuum of a single sentient being, there are the causal factors to be cultivated that comprise the gates of the three bodies; therefore, he is called "One Buddha.
Thus, the "thousand Śākyas" refers to the response body (nirmāṇakāya), while the "ten billion Śākyas" refers to the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya). This is known from the case of Vairocana.

Regarding the name being applied to all three bodies: in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, when the Bodhisattva who compiled the Dharma-piṭaka addressed the presiding teacher Śākyamuni Buddha of that time, he said, "I take refuge in the All-Knowing Ocean, Vairocana Buddha.
Thus, we know it refers to all [three bodies] collectively. As for "sitting upon the lotus pedestal," one should contemplate the world atop the lotus pedestal; as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"O Son of the Buddha, you should know that there are wind-circles as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru.
Among them, the lowest wind-circle that supports this Lotus Treasury Adorned World-Ocean is named 'Equanimity' (Samatā). It supports all the Radiance of Jewels.
Above it is the wind-circle named 'Adorned with Various Jewels' (Vicitraratnavyūha), which supports the Pure Light Jewel Pond, and so on, up to the highest wind-circle named..."
Jewel-Store Sustainer. Within all those seas of fragrant water, there is a great lotus named Fragrant Banner Light Adornment Sustainer.
On the edge of this Lotus Treasury Adorned World-Ocean, there is a mountain of diamond that encircles it on all sides.
Furthermore, beneath that ground, there are seas of fragrant water as numerous as the atoms within unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
Adorned with various jewels, its shores are made of all kinds of fragrant *maṇi* gems and precious stones.
Nets of precious stones cover it above, and waters of various jewel colors fill it to the brim. All manner of lotuses are in full bloom, and the water is perfumed with fine sandalwood powder.
The sublime voice of the Tathāgata resounds there constantly without ceasing. Each of these fragrant water-seas has four [features].
It is surrounded by celestial rivers of fragrant water and fine dust, with various precious flowers covering its surface. Below it says: "This is the Lotus Treasury World.
Within each and every realm, there are oceans of worlds as numerous as the atoms in an ocean of worlds, all purely adorned. O Son of the Buddha!"
Upon this Sea of Fragrant Water, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms of unspeakably many Buddha-fields.
As for the term "flower," it refers to the various worlds inhabited by the thousand Śākyamunis and others. As for the "pedestal" (*maṇḍala*), it represents the world where Vairocana Buddha dwells;
it is called a "pedestal" because it is intended to manifest the meaning of the "intermediate. Furthermore, within each petal are many worlds, all of which rest upon lotus flowers.
Regarding "the inclusion of worlds": there is nothing that is not the world of Lotus-Flower Above (Padmottara). Regarding "sitting upright": this refers to the correct principle.
Within the second section, among the assembly listening to the Dharma, there are three pairs.
First, from "surrounding" down to "attaining Buddhahood at once," the person and the Dharma are paired as a dyad. Second, from "thus" down to "one's own body," the fundamental and... [text ends]
The final two [lines] form a pair. Regarding the third [section], which proceeds from "thousands and hundreds" down to "multitudes as numerous as atoms," the Teacher and the followers form a pair.

Within the first [of these two], there are two parts: the first line clarifies the person who awakens, and the following two lines clarify the phenomena that are awakened to. Within the first of these, there are also two parts:
the first two lines represent the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), and the following two lines represent the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body). The first line clarifies abiding.

Location. The second line correctly clarifies the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). The initial phrase, "surrounding the thousand-petaled flower," clarifies that the response body dwells within the thousand pure lands.
As for what is called the "response body," this refers to the response body within the context of the "emanation gate" (*vibhakti-mukha*). The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:
"There are response bodies that are not transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is the meaning of "is. Second, within the clarification of the transformation body, there is indeed...

Second: The first phrase clarifies the dwelling place; the second phrase correctly clarifies the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). As for the statement "one flower, ten billion lands," this clarifies that the transformation bodies [reside] in ten billion lands such as Jambudvīpa.
Regarding "one Śākyamuni per land," this refers to the Śākyamuni within the context of the emanation gate (*vibhaktimukha*).
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "There are those who are exclusively transformation bodies and not response bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*). This refers to...

This is its meaning. Although the aforementioned Vairocana Buddha possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*), within the context of the three types of Buddhas, he is designated as the "True Body" (*dharmakāya*) in contrast to the exclusively responsive body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the exclusively transformational body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Second, regarding the clarification of the dharma that is realized, there are two parts: the first phrase clarifies the dwelling place, while the second phrase correctly expresses the dharma that is realized. As for what is said:

Regarding the Bodhi tree: "Bodhi" refers to both enlightenment (*bodhi*) and awakening. Because Prince Siddhārtha sat beneath this tree and attained supreme awakening, the tree under which he realized his awakening was designated by the name of that awakening;
thus it is called the Bodhi tree. As for "attaining the Way to Buddhahood at one time":
just as Śākyamuni attained the Way here in this world, Śākyamunis in other directions likewise all attain the Way within the same single period of time. Therefore...
Regarding the statement "attaining Buddhahood in a single moment":
in the second pair, the first phrase clarifies the end and the second phrase clarifies the beginning; the textual explanation is easily understood.
In the third pair, which contrasts the teacher with the followers, the first phrase designates the teacher and the second phrase reveals the followers—the multitude of subtle atoms.
As for this, the multitude gathered is incalculable; therefore, it is called "a multitude as numerous as motes of dust.
The third section, which sets forth the Dharma taught, consists of two parts. The first line clarifies that the assembly has arrived at the Buddha’s presence;
the following two lines clarify the specific Dharma being taught. Regarding the initial phrase, "all have come to my place": "all have come" means—
The assembly received by the thousand and ten billion Śākyamunis all came to the place of their original Lord; therefore, it is said that they "all came together.

Regarding the phrase "my own," this refers to the self of Vairocana Buddha. As for the statement that "the gate of ambrosia is opened," "ambrosia" (amṛta) is translated as the "medicine of immortality.
Concerning this, there are two explanations: first, it is because of the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*) which are expressed [by the teaching].

The Dharma is nectar (*amṛta*). By means of the teaching that explains it—namely, because by upholding the threefold aggregate of precepts one can obtain the deathless medicine of unsurpassed enlightenment—the explained Dharma of the threefold aggregate of precepts itself is taken as nectar. One version says:
Taking unsurpassed bodhi as the nectar and the three clusters of precepts as the gate. The meaning of "gate" has many aspects. First is the sense of entering and exiting.
This meaning of "gate" refers to the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) and the morality of gathering the true dharma (*dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*); these are the precepts for one's own benefit.
Therefore, it takes "entering" as its meaning. If it encompasses the various precepts, this is the practice of benefiting others;
therefore, it takes "exiting" as its meaning. One interpretation states that the meanings of "closing" and "hearing" constitute the meaning of a "gate.

That is to say, when an evil thief comes with the intent to seize the internal wealth, [the gate] can cause him to be shut out and prevented from entering; thus, it takes "closing" as its meaning. The precepts are likewise.
This is so because it functions as a "gate" (dvāra) by means of the two gateways of the prohibitory precepts (*śīla*) and the prescriptive precepts (*śīla*).

When the thieves of transgressions—both those of omission and those of commission—seek to enter and plunder the wealth of the precepts, these gates cause them to turn back and retreat; thus, they cannot enter to seize it.

Because this meaning is still manifest, it is called a "gate. Alternatively, if one takes "opening and revealing" to be the meaning of a gate: when a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of like mind enters, [the gate opens].
In the middle, it can open the gate and close it; it also causes the internal wealth to arise because of the mind of aspiration. Thus, revealing [what was hidden] is taken as the meaning of "gate.

The precepts are also like this: by personally upholding the three clusters of precepts (*triskandhaka-śīla*), one is able to perceive the Buddha-nature, the *tathāgatagarbha*, and original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*) within, even reaching the supreme jewel-wealth of the fruit of Buddhahood on the tenth stage. This is also due to opening [the gate].

Because it is the gateway to the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*), it is able to cause other sentient beings to also perceive the Buddha-nature and original enlightenment (*prakṛti-vijñāna*), up to the inner treasure-wealth of the fruit of Buddhahood; thus, "opening and revealing" constitutes the meaning of the "gateway.
Within the three sections of the introduction, the introduction concerning Vairocana Buddha has already been concluded above.
At this time, from "Below the thousand and hundred" onwards, there is a second section concerning the Śākyas of other directions, which consists of four parts:

first, one line and one verse of verse explaining how each of the Buddhas recites; second, from "The precepts are like the sun and moon" onwards, one line of verse praising the virtue of the precepts;
third, from "This is what Rocana recites" onwards, five lines of verse clarifying the exhortation to beings.

Receive and uphold it. Fourth, the entire assembly is urged with respect, concluding the exhortation. Of these [verses], the first two lines clarify returning to the original site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);
the latter two lines correctly clarify the recitation of the precepts. At the beginning of the precepts, the term "site of enlightenment" is used as a metaphorical designation.
This means that within the world, a "site" (*maṇḍa*) refers to a place where one gathers the essence from sugar; thus it is called a "site. The site of enlightenment is likewise so named.
This is so. Because one is able to abandon the three obstructions and take up the site of Bodhi, it is called the "site of the Way" (bodhimaṇḍa).

Regarding the recitation of the precepts of our Original Teacher, there are two explanations. One says: because they were originally taught by Vairocana, they are called the "precepts of the Original Teacher. Another says:
since all Buddhas likewise take the precepts as their teacher, they are called the "precepts of the Original Teacher."
In the second section, the Praise of Virtue, there are two parts. The first two lines clarify the praise of the virtue of precepts by employing a metaphor;

the latter two lines praise the precepts by citing their essential qualities. Within the initial praise of precepts through metaphor, the statement "the precepts are like the sun and moon" contains, in brief, three meanings:
first, because the very nature of the sun and moon is free from defilement and is luminously pure, they are also able to dispel the darkness of others. And...

Regarding actual entities, the precepts are likewise so. Because their intrinsic nature is free from defilement and is luminously pure, they are able to shatter the dark obstructions of the afflictions and black dharmas, and because they manifest and reveal such entities as the Buddha-nature and the Tathāgatagarbha, they correspond to the meaning of the sun and moon;
thus, they serve as metaphors. Second, the sun has heat as its nature, while the moon has coldness as its nature. If there were a sun but no...

As for the moon: if the myriad sprouts are scorched and withered, they cannot produce fruit. Likewise, if there were a moon but no sun, the myriad plants and things would rot and thus could not produce shoots.

The precepts are also like this: if one possesses the precept of restraining oneself (*saṃvara-śīla*) and the precept of gathering the true Dharma (*dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), yet lacks the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*), there is only practice for one's own benefit and no benefit for others.
Because they practice other [paths], they are the same as those of the two vehicles and do not produce the abundant fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.

If one possesses the precept of gathering sentient beings but lacks the precepts of gathering discipline and gathering wholesome dharmas, there is only benefit for others and no practice for self-benefit;
thus, one is still the same as an ordinary person and cannot produce the sprout of bodhi. Now, as for being complete...
Because there are the sun and the moon, sprouts and seedlings can neither rot nor wither. Precepts are likewise:

because they fully possess the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*), one is able to differ from ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, and is able to bring forth the threefold fruit of unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Therefore, the sun and moon are used as a metaphor. Although the sun and moon soar through the sky far removed from the earth, they remain unattached to empty space.

The precepts are likewise: because a bodhisattva can maintain the three clusters of precepts that avoid extremes, and because they can remain free from the view of existence, although they manifest soaring within the empty space of the *dharmatā*, they remain unattached to the view of emptiness. The sun...
The moon possesses these three meanings; likewise, the three clusters of precepts (tri-skandha-śīla) fully possess these three meanings.
Therefore, the sun and moon are used as metaphors. It is also like a jeweled necklace:
even if a person’s physical form is unattractive, if they adorn their body with precious necklaces, they will be respected and admired by all people.

Virtue. Precepts are also like this. Although precepts may become "ugly conduct" due to the practice of unwholesome actions, if one is able to guard and uphold the three groups of precepts (tri-skandha-śīla), one will attain the virtue of being respected and envied by all humans and devas;

therefore, they are likened to a necklace (*hāra*). As the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*) states: "Among the six classes of bodhisattvas and the twenty-seven noble ones (*ārya*), there is the Necklace."
It adorns the body; the meaning is also like this. By means of the three clusters of precepts and the fifty mental states, the bodhisattva and the Buddha take them as necklaces (*keyūra*).
As for the term "beads," the treatise refers to the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).

If a person obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel and holds it in their hand, whatever they desire from among the myriad treasures will be obtained without exception. The precepts are also like this. If one...

For those who have reached the pearl of precepts through the hand of faith, all the myriad treasures of mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas—whatever they may wish for—are obtained without exception;

therefore, the pearl is used as a metaphor. One interpretation states that the first phrase represents the adornment of wisdom (*prajñā-alaṃkāra*) and the second phrase represents the adornment of merit (*puṇya-alaṃkāra*).

Another interpretation states that the metaphors of the sun and moon represent the internal virtues such as the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*). As for the *ratna-hāra* (jeweled necklace)...
"Necklace" (ruò) refers to not only possessing internal virtue, but also being able to possess external virtues such as the adornment of the physical body;

therefore, it is used as a metaphor for a necklace (*keyūra*). "Jewel" (zhū) refers to not only possessing internal and external virtues, but also being able to possess the sovereign virtue of utilizing the jewels of the mundane and supramundane wholesome dharmas;
therefore, it is used as a metaphor for a jewel (*maṇi*). The multitude of subtle-dust Bodhisattvas [is] analyzed.

The great earth consists of as many atoms as there are grains of dust. Because they uphold the precepts, those who have attained the state of a Perfectly Enlightened One (Samyaksambuddha) are likewise as numerous as these atoms;
therefore, it is said that there is a multitude of Bodhisattvas as numerous as atoms. Those who have thus attained perfect enlightenment are like snakes:
although their nature is to move in curves, when they enter a bamboo tube, they naturally become straight. Sentient beings are also like this; from [the beginningless]... [without end].

At the outset, because one has practiced erroneous intentions, one becomes established in an improper nature. However, if one enters the governance of the threefold aggregate of precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), one spontaneously achieves perfect enlightenment;

therefore, it is said that "by means of this, one achieves perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, regarding these threefold aggregates of precepts: the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint) is the heading for the virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*);

the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas) is the heading for the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*); and the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings) [is the heading for the virtue of compassion].
This refers to the "eyes of grace. Because of these three eyes, one attains the fruit of the three virtues; therefore, it is said that "by this, perfect enlightenment is achieved.
The three virtues are unified to constitute the fruit of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Thus, the praise of the virtue of ethical discipline (*śīla*) concludes with the preceding section.

From this point onward, Vairocana recites the third section, which exhorts beings to accept and uphold [the teaching]. This section also consists of two parts: the first two lines cite his own example to provide the exhortation;
the subsequent passage beginning with "You, newly initiated bodhisattvas... constitutes the formal exhortation for you all to accept and uphold it.
Within the formal exhortation, there are further two parts: the first three lines of verse exhort the assembly present at that time, while the following portion exhorting all sentient beings...

The section beginning with "The mind" consists of one and a half verses, which serves as a general exhortation for the assembly of both worlds. This segment is also titled "Exhorting Beings by Highlighting Benefits.

Within this initial section for the contemporary assembly, there are also three parts: first, two lines exhorting oneself to uphold [the precepts]; second, two lines exhorting others to transmit them;
third, from "Listen attentively" onwards, exhorting the emergence of the three types of wisdom through listening to the precepts. The middle portion clarifies these three.

Wisdom consists of three stages. First, the initial three phrases encourage the emergence of *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from hearing). Second, from "The great assembly believes with a sincere heart" onwards, it encourages the emergence of *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from reflection).
Third, from "Always maintain such faith" onwards, it encourages the emergence of *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom derived from cultivation).
Regarding the first stage, the statement "I also recite thus" refers to me, Śākyamuni, of another direction.
In the second section, "Right Exhortation," regarding the term "to wear upon the crown": within the physical body (*rūpakāya*), the crown is the most superior part;

thus, it is used here to illustrate the meaning of wearing [the teaching] upon the crown of one's faith. Regarding the distinction between "receiving" (*udgraha*) and "upholding" (*dhāraṇa*), the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* provides three successive explanations.
First: if one receives the precepts from another, it is called "receiving"; if one attains the precepts through one's own mind, it is called "upholding. The commentary explains: if from another...

First, one who has not previously received [the precepts] now receives them; thus it is called "receiving. If one attains the precepts through one's own mind, one must first be a person who maintains the precepts within the past [continuum] before they can be attained;
because the precepts are attained through one's own mind, it is called "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*). Second, that which exists prior [to the formal act] is termed "receiving."

Holding [the teachings] thereafter is called "retention" (*dhāraṇī*). Third, practicing and maintaining the precepts is called "receiving" (*samādāna*). If one memorizes and maintains the words and phrases, this is called "retention.
Regarding what is termed "listening attentively" (*śuśrūṣamāṇa*), there are three meanings: first, the meaning of non-distraction; second, the meaning of the supreme naturelessness;
and third, the meaning of being free from turbidity—these constitute the sense of "listening attentively. For example, it is like an overturned vessel: even if rain falls, it will ultimately...
It cannot receive [the teaching]; this corresponds to the meaning of distraction. Or it is like a vessel with holes; although it receives the rain from heaven, it can never retain it.
This corresponds to the meaning of contemptuousness. It is also like a soiled vessel; although it can retain water, others will not use it.
This meaning corresponds to the meaning of turbidity. "Because it enables one to depart from these three faults" means:

"Listen attentively to these words above. Regarding those who have received and upheld these precepts," the teacher explains: "If one is at the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), although they are beginners learning the precepts, they are unable to maintain their station.
Only from the Ten Understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) upward do they uphold the precepts according to their capacity.

It is only from the First Ground (*prathamā-bhūmi*) upward that one can truly be called 'one who upholds the precepts. As for upholding the precepts with ultimate purity, one attains this name only upon reaching the Second Ground."
Regarding the observance of the precepts: this stage constitutes the perfection of the stage of the *śīla-pāramitā*.
For those below this stage, although they do not intentionally violate the precepts, there is the possibility of accidental transgressions; therefore, they cannot be called ultimately pure.

As for those who receive, uphold, and transmit [the teachings] to other sentient beings: if they are persons of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), they must not transmit them to others. Persons at this stage...
One studies the precepts for ten kalpas; only those of the tenth stage or above attain the station of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Therefore, the precepts are conferred upon those of the lower stages. Nevertheless, those below the stages who possess the emptiness of persons and are free from outflows (*anāsrava*) are all similar;

they merely receive the transformation according to their respective capacities. As for the ultimate station of transformation, it is only upon the stages (*bhūmi*) that one attains transformation, having attained true non-outflow.
Regarding the stage of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), there are two explanations within the Buddha-dharma concerning the "Treasury of Precepts" (*śīlaskandha*).

One states that the teaching which expresses [the precepts] constitutes the treasury, as it refers to the Vinaya-piṭaka among the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*). Another states that these three clusters of precepts constitute a "treasury" because they possess the sense of encompassing and containing various practices such as concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The meaning of the three types of wisdom is as commonly explained. As for what is called *pratimokṣa*:

The translated name is "Liberation Everywhere. Because the meaning of liberation exists within both the causal and resultant stages—specifically, because it precludes non-virtue among the three types of action during the causal stage—it is called "liberation" in the sense that it possesses the capacity to be free from bondage.

Furthermore, because one can attain the resultant liberation of unsurpassed *bodhi* by upholding the three clusters of vows (*tri-śikṣā*), it is also called "liberation. You are one who shall become [this].
A "Buddha" is so called because, by means of upholding the precepts, one possesses the cause for attaining Buddhahood; since the fruit arises from the cause, one is named a "future Buddha.
As for me, I am one who has already attained Buddhahood, demonstrating that I achieved it through the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-pada*).
This citation encourages others by pointing to the benefits gained by oneself. One who constantly maintains such faith will, regardless of circumstances, always be free from [transgressions].
Because of faith, it is said that one always maintains such faith. Regarding the phrase "the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*) is already complete," there are two explanations.

First, it is said that because the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is fulfilled in the second stage (*bhūmi*), it is called the completion of the aggregate of ethical discipline. Second, it is said that "aggregate" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of "category" (*prakāra*). It is not merely the attainment of ethical discipline;
rather, by virtue of upholding the precepts, one is also able to attain the practices of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*) and so forth. Therefore, it is called an "aggregate."
The section beginning with "All those who possess a mind" and following, which cites benefits to exhort sentient beings, also consists of three parts.

First, the initial three phrases cite oneself to provide exhortation; next, two phrases cite those of high status to provide exhortation; finally, one phrase cites true sons of the Buddha to provide exhortation.

Regarding the first point, "all those who possess a mind," this refers to the primary cause of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings, whether ordinary..."
Those who possess a mind shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Generally, those who possess a mind have two kinds of mind:

first, the *tathatā*-mind; this mind, from the very beginning, is fully endowed with qualities and virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and is therefore called the "non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Second, the mind of arising and ceasing; as for this mind—
Because it is obscured by afflictions, its nature does not manifest; thus, in the sense of being hidden, it is called "emptiness.

However, when free from defilement, it flows forth with the meaning of "thickness" (substantiality), and is therefore also called the *tathāgatagarbha*. For example, although water forms waves, it never loses its essential nature as water;
hence it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*. This refers to the *tathāgatagarbha* that is currently hidden and covered, yet manifests as the Dharma.
All sentient beings possess these two kinds of mind; therefore, they are called "all those who possess a mind. Regarding "embracing the Buddha-precepts":

"embracing" (shè) has the meaning of "taking up" or "gathering in. This means entering the rank of all Buddhas. As for "having attained a rank identical to that of Great Enlightenment," the Vinaya Master says:
since one has entered the ranks from the first bhūmi upward, it is said that one enters the rank of all Buddhas; for all ten bhūmis constitute Buddhahood.
This is because it pertains to the stages (*bhūmi*), as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. The Teacher says:

"Because one attains the fruit through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and because one is able to enter the state of Buddhahood as the future fruit by means of embracing the three aggregates of precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*), it is said that one 'immediately enters the stage of all Buddhas.'"

"Having attained a rank equal to Great Enlightenment"—as for the term "Great Enlightenment," it refers to that which is not a partial or concordant awakening; therefore, it is called Great Enlightenment.

"Truly being a child of the Buddhas" refers to Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), and thus they are called true children of the Buddha, because they possess the fourfold meaning of being a child of the Buddha.
Regarding what is called the fourfold meaning of being a child of the Buddha, as for the general designation "child of the Buddha," it is based on...

The metaphor is used for the sake of designation. That is to say, one who is a prince of the wheel-turning monarch succeeds to the position in the sequence of the text and thereby assumes the sovereignty over the four continents.
A bodhisattva is likewise; being able to succeed to the position of a Buddha and thereby assume the singular station of the Dharma-realm, they are called a "Son of the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "seed of the mind," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "First, taking faith as the seed; by means of this..."
Because of faith, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood; by means of this mind, one is able to counteract the obstacle of the icchantika’s lack of faith.

As for its stage, it pertains to the stage of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Second, because it takes Prajñā as its mother, it is able to counteract the obstacle of non-Buddhists’ attachment to a self;
this corresponds to the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*). Third, because it takes meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) as its womb, it is able to...
It remedies the obstacles of suffering for the assembly of śrāvakas; this refers to the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

Fourth, because it takes great compassion as its nurse, it can remedy the obstacle of the mind of renunciation characteristic of pratyekabuddhas; this refers to the stage of the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).

Although these four meanings exist within the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi, they are merely similar [to the true state], and thus one cannot be called a true son of the Buddha. From the first bhūmi onward...
The aforementioned possesses four meanings; furthermore, because it is the reality itself and not a mere semblance, one is called a "true son of the Buddha.
The passage beginning with "The great assembly all pay respect" constitutes the fourth section, which serves as a summary and exhortation. Regarding the term "respect":
to yield one's own virtues to those above is called "reverence" (gōng); to offer salutation to those above through the three karmas of body, speech, and mind is called "veneration" (jìng).
From "At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha" below, this is the third section: the introduction concerning Śākyamuni of this world. It consists of two parts:
first, the introduction provided by the scribe of the sutra; second, from "He addressed the various bodhisattvas" below, the introduction provided by the Buddha.

Within the former, there are also three sections: first, the explanation of the Buddha’s formulation of the precepts; second, the explanation of the emission of light; third, the explanation of the assembly listening to the Dharma. Text.
This can be seen in the text. First, within the explanation of the formulation of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*), there are also two sections: first, the person who is able to interrogate;

second, from the initial formulation of the precept downward, which represents the dharma that is being formulated. Within the representation of the dharma being formulated, there are also three sections:

first, from the initial formulation downward, representing the name of the formulated precept; second, from "filial obedience" (*kṣānti*) downward, distinguishing the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the precept; third...

From the words "Filial piety is named" (*xiào míng yǐ xià*) onwards, the names of the precepts are explained. Within the second section, which discriminates the essence (*ti*), there are also two parts:

first, the formal clarification of the essence of the precepts; second, the clarification of the functional efficacy of the precepts' activities. Regarding the initial phrase "at that time" (*ěrshí*), it is easily understood.

As for "Śākyamuni": Śākya is his clan name; Muni is his personal name. Translated, it means "Capable Benevolence" (*néng rén*). He is called "Capable Benevolence" because he is capable of being benevolent toward sentient beings. If one follows the *Zá*... [text fragment ends]
Regarding the "Proponent of Mind" (Cittavādin) and Kāśyapa Muni: his body, speech, and mind are perfected. This means that among the three karmas, his actions accord with wisdom;

there is nothing therein that is not complete. As for his initial sitting beneath the Bodhi tree and attaining unsurpassed enlightenment, the Teacher says this is not an explanation based on the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), but is discussed in terms of the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya) and Transformation-body (saṃbhogakāya). This can be understood accordingly. Thus it is called "unsurpassed."
Regarding "Awakening" (*buddha*): although those below the [first] stage possess the sense of awakening, it is merely similar [to it].
Although Bodhisattvas of the ten stages possess awakening, because this is an awakening that is only partial (*yathābhāga*), it cannot be called "unsurpassed awakening.

Since the Buddha has already perfected the realization of the Path, in order to distinguish him from the two preceding types of awakening, he is called "Unsurpassed Awakening. This concludes the initial section on the Bodhisattva *Prātimokṣa*.

Regarding the *Kṣa* (the *Kṣudraka-āgama*), there are two traditions. The Vinaya masters say there are two traditions: one says it was taught after the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, while another says it was taught before the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

The Teachers say that, according to the Hīnayāna, from the time the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment until the thirty-seventh day, he first taught the *Sūtras* in the Deer Park; for twelve years thereafter, he taught [the *Vinaya*].
Regarding the *Vinaya*: if one belongs to the Mahāyāna, immediately upon attaining the Way, one first establishes these precepts and likewise first expounds the *Sūtras*.

As for "filial piety" (*xiàosùn*): it is the meaning of non-contradiction in practice; this is the meaning of filial conduct. This meaning is in accord with the principle of "accordance" (*shùn*). Within this, there are three explanations.

First, it is said that the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint) constitutes filial piety, while the *dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering the true Dharma) and the *sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering sentient beings) [constitute the other two].
Precepts are the means of compliance. Second, taking the essence of receiving the precepts as filial piety (*hiao*), and taking the practice of following them as compliance (*shun*).

Third, taking the unmanifested precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*) as filial piety, and taking the manifested precepts (*vijñapti-śīla*) as compliance. Regarding "parents," there are two explanations. One says:

there are causal parents, such as those who exist in the secular world; there are parents for entering the Path, referring to the three teachers and so forth; and regarding the Sangha, it refers to...

Regarding the remaining seven types of practitioners and so forth: the term "teacher" (*śāstr*) refers to an individual practitioner who adopts individual conduct; the term "monastic community" (*saṃgha*) refers to the collective of monks who adopt communal conduct.

Since the practice of filial piety alone generally does not involve departing from the community to engage in these two distinct modes of conduct, it does not conflict with either communal or individual conduct.

Therefore, it is said that one should be filial and obedient toward one's preceptors and monks. Regarding the term "Three Jewels" (Triratna), there are many approaches to distinguishing their individual characteristics within their single essence;
for now, however, we shall manifest their characteristics according to one particular approach. As for these individual characteristics: the Three Bodies (Trikāya) are taken as the Buddha Jewel.
The Dharma Jewel consists of the teachings of the Three Piṭakas as they have been expounded. The Saṃgha Jewel consists of the assemblies of the Three Vehicles.
Regarding their identity: within the Buddha, the sense of awakening constitutes the Buddha Jewel; because he provides no standard for others to follow, it is called the Dharma Jewel.
The Buddha is able to transcend strife and conflict and accords with the Middle Way; therefore, he is called the Jewel of the Saṃgha. Regarding the Dharma of the Ultimate Path of Filial Piety:
because it reaches the ultimate path-dharma of the Dharma-realm, it is called the Dharma of the Ultimate Path. "Filial piety" is termed *śīla* (precept);

because it can admonish and restrain non-virtue within the three karmas, it is named precept (*śīla*). It is also termed "restraint," because by means of the *saṃvara-śīla* (vow-precept), one is able to restrain [unwholesome conduct].
It is because of the precepts for gathering the True Dharma and gathering sentient beings that one is able to restrain transgressions and non-virtues; therefore, it is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*).

Because it restrains what is non-virtuous, it can cause one to abide in wholesome dharmas; therefore, it is called "stopping" (*niyama*). As for "emitting light from the mouth," this refers to the second section.
Since he wishes to preach the dharma of the precepts through the action of speech, he must emit light from his mouth; it is not for [any other purpose].
Because he intended for other karmic results, he did not emit further rays of light. At that time, there were fewer than one million people in the third assembly listening to the Dharma.
Regarding the eighteen Brahmās: since there are three in each of the lower three dhyānas, that makes nine;
and because there are nine in the fourth dhyāna, there are eighteen Brahmā heavens. The six desire heavens are the six heavens of the desire realm. As for the Buddha’s Great Precepts:
Regarding this "Bodhisattva Precept": it is called the "Great Precept" (Mahā-śīla) in comparison to the precepts of the Hīnayāna.
From the words "Addressing all Bodhisattvas" onwards is the second section, the Buddha’s introduction, which contains three parts:

first, the exhortation to recite oneself; second, from "Therefore, the light of the precepts... onwards, a brief elucidation of the characteristics of the precepts; and third, from "O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively... onwards.

Below, the recipients of the precepts are listed in detail. The initial statement, "I now recite [the precepts] every half-month myself," is intended to manifest that I take the precepts as my teacher;
thus, I constantly recite the precepts of which I am the teacher. If you all likewise take the precepts as your teacher, [you should do the same].
It may also be recited; thus it is said, "I now recite. Regarding the phrase "reciting every half-month," this is stated in reference to the Sangha Jewel.
If one were to apply this to an individual practitioner—a bodhisattva of recent resolve who has not yet mastered the recitation—they would recite six times during the course of a single day.
Within the monastic law, what does "reciting every half-month" mean? It means reciting repeatedly.

This is because people’s minds give rise to contempt. It is said that the minds of worldly people regard those with few practices as venerable, while they treat those who are profound as insignificant.
Furthermore, just as one who performs few deeds cannot increase the Dharma, one must abandon both scarcity and excess and adopt the Middle Way;
therefore, it is necessary to recite the precepts every half-month. As for the Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind, this refers to the stage of the Ten Faiths.

Regarding the "ten stages of setting forth" (*daśa-prasthāna*): these are established in reference to the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*). Why are the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) not considered stages of setting forth?
It is because although Bodhisattvas at this stage possess an understanding of emptiness, they have not yet set out toward actual practice; therefore, they are not called stages of setting forth.

For this reason, Bodhisattvas of the ten faiths are termed "Bodhisattvas by name" (*nāma-bodhisattva*) or "provisional Bodhisattvas. Question: What is the sequential relationship between the ten faiths and the ten understandings?
There is no meaning in exceeding the stages. Why, then, are they established as far as the stage of "letters" (*vyañjana*)? Answer:

From the stage of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) up to the stage of the fixed group (*niyata-rāśi*), they are thus established as far as the stage of "letters. Question: According to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*, those in the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are like light feathers;
therefore, they are subject to regression and do not enter the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. However, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, [they do]. [End of fragment]
"The stage of non-retrogression" and "entering the count of the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas"—how are these two passages to be reconciled? Answer:

If one follows the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* to interpret this text: if a person of bodhisattva-nature enters the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), they attain non-retrogression at the very moment they enter the first faith.
However, if a person of the two-vehicle (*dvaya-yāna*) nature turns from the small toward the great, they do not yet enter [the stage of non-retrogression] during the ten stages of faith.

The stage of non-retrogression has not yet entered the count of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. It is only upon reaching the stage of the ten understandings (*daśa-vijñapti*) that one attains the stage of non-retrogression and enters the count of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Therefore, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (Renwang jing) designates this as a stage of retrogression with respect to those of the nature of the two vehicles (*dviyāna-gotra*).
Conversely, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* designates it as a stage of non-retrogression with respect to those of the Bodhisattva nature (*bodhisattva-gotra*).

Regarding those who transcend the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) states: "Those of the superior grade attain the transcendence of the ten faiths within one or two kalpas;
as for those of the lowest grade, they must pass through an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) before they can attain the transcendence of faith.
This is explained extensively even in the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. As for this dharma of precepts: if one discusses the bodhicitta, it constitutes the first faith; if one discusses the precepts...
The "mind" refers to the sixth stage, the mind of precepts (*śīlacitta*). The "ten nurturings" (*daśa-poṣadha*) correspond to the ten stages of understanding (*daśa-adhimukti*).

The "ten vajras" correspond to the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmana*); because they cannot be moved by external conditions, they are called the "ten vajras. This is a name derived from a metaphor.

From this point onward, the second section briefly explains the characteristics of the precepts (*śīla*). This section consists of three parts: first, clarifying the causes and conditions of the precepts;
second, clarifying the fulfillment of the essence of the precepts; and third, from "the root of all Buddhas" onwards, clarifying the benefits of the precepts.

Regarding the initial phrase "light of the precepts," it is a metaphorical designation. It means that the precepts are bright and pure because they are free from defilement, and they are also capable of destroying darkness.

Therefore, it possesses a meaning similar to light; thus, it is named after its metaphor. In the initial clarification of the causes and conditions of the precepts, the statement "there are conditions, not no cause" means that there are the three *karmas* (formal procedures) as well as the conditions of the teacher and the Sangha; hence, it is said "there are conditions.
"Not no cause" means that the causes for generating the three grades of bodhicitta are not absent; hence, it is said "not no cause."

In the second section, which analyzes the essence [of the teaching], regarding the term "light and light" (*guāngguāng*), there are several explanations. First, it is said that within the light emitted, there are also immeasurable lights;
therefore, it is called "light and light. Second, it is said that it is called "light" because light is emitted, and because the precepts (*śīladharma*) are also taught by means of that light.

Therefore, it is said "light and light" (*ābhā-ābhā*). One interpretation states: regarding the precepts explained in the treatise, there are differences between the active (*vijñapti*) and the non-active (*avijñapti*), hence it is said "light and light.

Another interpretation states: this expresses the difference between the two types of precepts—the formal undertaking (*samādāna*) and the subsequent observance (*anuvartana*)—hence it is said "light and light.

Yet another interpretation states: because the three clusters of precepts (*triskandha-śīla*) are not one, it is said "light and light. Furthermore, one should also say that within each cluster there are immeasurable precepts; therefore, it is said [“light and light”].
Radiant, radiant! It is neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black. Black is unwholesome; blue and the other four colors are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

As for the essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) described in the treatises, it is neither evil nor indeterminate, because it is wholesome. Thus it is said to be "neither blue, yellow, red, white, nor black.
It is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), because the meaning of "precept" consists in the prevention of wrongdoing and the cessation of evil. This...
Precepts, although arising from form (*rūpa*), are not form; although arising from mind (*citta*), they are not mind. Therefore, it is said that they are neither form nor mind.
According to the Abhidharma of the Hīnayāna schools, there are "factors dissociated from both form and mind" (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) which possess actual existence and substantial essence;
thus, they are termed "neither form nor mind. As for the essence of these precepts, it consists solely of the principle of preventing what is improper.

Therefore, because it does not have the sense of being substantial (*dravya*), because it does not have the sense of being matter (*rūpa*) or a conditioned object (*ālambana*), and because it is not the mind (*citta*), there are differing explanations regarding the three types of action (*trikarma*) that constitute the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).
According to the *Sabhāṣya*, the fourfold agent has as its essence invisible and non-obstructive matter (*anidarśanam apratigham rūpam*).

Because it is obtained by the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*): if it is the form (*rūpa*) subsumed under the sense-base of sound (*śabda-āyatana*), its essence is visible and resistant form, because it is obtained by the eye-consciousness (*cakṣur-vijñāna*) and is thus subsumed under the sense-base of form (*rūpa-āyatana*). If it is the non-informative restraint (*avijñapti-śīla*), its essence is invisible and non-resistant form;
this is because it is obtained by the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) and is thus subsumed under the sense-base of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*). According to the Satyasiddhi school:

As for this, the *vijñapti-śīla* (active precept) takes volition (*cetanā*) as its substance. Physical and vocal forms (*rūpa*) are not, in themselves, the substance of the precept, because such form is invariably indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Since form lacks the nature of demerit or merit, it is not the substance of the precept. If one speaks of *avijñapti-śīla* (non-active precept), it takes that which is neither form nor mind as its substance.
According to the Mahāyāna school, if one considers the general perspective, the *vijñapti-śīla* generally takes the three types of action (*tri-karma*) as its substance. This is...
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* asks: "What is the essence (*svabhāva*) of these three types of precepts? It answers:

"Their essence consists of the non-arising of afflictions, the absence of the intention to harm others, and the performance of wholesome bodily, vocal, and mental actions. If one analyzes them by their specific nature, they have mental action as their essence.
A passage from the *Saṃgraha* states: "Mental action is the essence. If [an action] arises through the gateway of speech, it is called vocal [action].
Regarding karma: if it arises through the gateway of the body, it is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*).

As for non-manifest action (*avijñapti*), according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, its essence consists of the perfuming (*vāsanā*) within the ālayavijñāna; according to the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-śāstra*, its essence consists of seeds (*bīja*).
Regarding that which is neither existent nor non-existent, the present precepts represent the Middle Way that transcends extremes. When discussing the essence of the precepts, they arise from causes.
Because it arises dependently, when one investigates its causes and conditions, the intrinsic nature of the precepts cannot be found; therefore, they are not existent.

Yet, because they arise from causes and conditions, although the precepts are non-existent, they are not like the horns of a rabbit which do not exist at all; thus, they are said to be non-non-existent. If one discusses the activity of the precepts:

There is the meaning of "preventing" regarding this precept; that which is prevented is this transgression. Since both the precept and the transgression arise from causes and conditions, one also seeks their causes and conditions, yet they are all unfindable.
That is to say, if one discusses the mind, its intrinsic nature is pure and thus not the nature of transgression.

Furthermore, both the object to be prevented and the non-transgression lack intrinsic nature, and therefore are not transgressions. Although they do not exist, they are also not non-existent; thus, it is able to—

This accords with the Middle Way. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Because neither transgression nor non-transgression can be apprehended, this is called being fully endowed with the *śīlapāramitā*.
If someone clings to the gate of non-existence as being existence, although they do not lose their precepts, they do not know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the precepts;
thus, they have committed an offense. If someone clings to the gate of non-existence...
Regarding those who hold the view of non-existence (*nāstika*), because they disparage the causal law of the precepts, they immediately lose their precepts.

To avoid these two extremes and accord with the Middle Way, it is said that [the precepts] are neither existent nor non-existent. Regarding that which is not the causal law, there are three explanations.
One interpretation states: because cause and effect cannot be apprehended, it is called a "non-cause-and-effect dharma. Another interpretation states:
it is not a mundane law of cause and effect, but rather a supramundane law of cause and effect; therefore, it is called a "non-cause-and-effect dharma. A third interpretation states:

regarding the seed that is the primary focus of the *vijñapti* (informative) precept, the essence of the *avijñapti* (non-informative) precept has two meanings: first, the meaning of preventing wrongdoing; second, the meaning of merit.

That seeds can produce the fruit of Buddhahood is the meaning of "merit within the family of precepts" (*śīla-kula*). That they can prevent what is non-virtuous is the meaning of "precepts within the family of merit.
Therefore, it is only through the meaning of "merit within the family of precepts" that one is able to produce the fruit of Buddhahood; this is the meaning of cause and effect.
To prevent what is non-virtuous within the "great family of merit" is not the meaning of the Buddha’s cause and effect; therefore, it is said to be "not cause and effect."
It is the Dharma. Question: Regarding the definition of *śīla* (precept) as the prevention of unwholesome acts within the continuum of the seeds, is this established as a designation upon the seeds?
Answer: No; it is not established as a designation upon the seeds. Rather, the entire substance [of the continuum] constitutes the seeds, and the entire substance also constitutes the precepts.
Question: If that is so, when the precepts are lost, are the subsequent seeds also lost? Answer: Although there is no difference in their substance, the seeds...
In the gate of the precepts within the family of the child, all is extinguished; in the seed-gate of the family of the precepts, the entire substance is not extinguished. It is like water and waves:
although they are originally distinct entities, when the wind ceases, the gate of the waves is entirely extinguished, while the gate of the water is entirely unextinguished.
Although this is the general explanation, if one distinguishes according to the three poisons regarding the arising of false views, there is merit within the family of the precepts.

In the case of the precepts of the Householder of Meaning and Merit, both [the meaning of the precept and the merit] are extinguished. If it is one with a mind of anger, only the meaning of the precept is extinguished while the meaning of the merit is not extinguished.
Other losses of the meaning of the precept are explained in detail later in the section on the precept of acting as a teacher for the sake of profit.

Now, regarding the loss of the precept, if one received them all at once—because they were received simultaneously through the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual)—and then gives rise to an intensified affliction (*kleśa*), one commits a single [offense].

When it is heavy, it is lost immediately. If one receives it according to its parts, because one formally undertakes each individual item during the act of receiving, even if one commits an offense through the arousal of intense afflictions, only that specific precept which was violated is lost; the remaining precepts are not lost.
Third, regarding the discernment of the benefits of the precepts: "The source of all Buddhas" indicates the causes performed in the past;
"the root of the practice of Bodhisattvas" indicates the root of what Bodhisattvas will perform in the future;
and "the root of the multitude of Buddhas" indicates that Bodhisattvas in the present serve as the root. As for "should be upheld," the ways of upholding are not the same, as follows:

Regarding what was stated previously, there are two interpretations concerning the phrase "should recite and study well" (*svādhyāya-śikṣita*). One says: "Reciting the text is called 'recitation' (*svādhyāya*); studying its meaning is called 'studying well' (*śikṣita*). Another says:

"Reciting the text, its meaning, and practicing them is called 'recitation'; if one can uphold the precepts for gathering and sustaining sentient beings through the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), that is [the true sense of] recitation."

Because one can uphold and gather the precepts of the True Dharma through the three types of wisdom, and uphold the precepts of restraint through the three roots of goodness, it is said that "one has learned well.

From the passage "O Son of the Buddha, listen attentively" onwards, there are three parts within the introduction: first, clarifying the self-exhortation; second, clarifying the emission of light, which concludes with the preceding section.

Below this, the third section lists those who receive the precepts. Regarding "eunuchs" (*paṇḍaka*), there are six types; that is, the six kinds of persons including those who are naturally so, those who are castrated, and so forth.
Regarding the "eight classes of spirits," each of the four heavenly kings leads two groups, such as the *yakṣas* and others.
Therefore, there are the two, four, and eight classes, as well as those who are emanations—such as devas, nāgas, and spirits—and those who have come as emanations to receive the bodhisattva precepts.
Question: For what reason are the beings of the formless realm not included? Answer: They may also be said to be included among the "emanations."
By including those permitted above, all may receive the precepts within the Mahāyāna. As for the obstacles and prohibitions of the Hīnayāna, they can be understood from their respective categories.
Regarding the statement above that there are two kinds of Vajra Deities: the first are those who can manifest divine bodies to protect the Dharma;
the second are those for whom the footprint of the Buddha at Liushi (Liu-shih) serves as the Vajra Deity. Regarding the person who receives the Bodhisattva precepts, Master Longjing said:

Only those in the human realm can properly receive [the precepts]. As for the aforementioned animals, eunuchs, spirits, ghosts, and so forth, this is spoken provisionally with reference to bodhisattvas and others who, through the power of their vows and their transformative manifestations (*nirmāṇa*), appear in various forms.

However, because they wish to once again clarify and reveal the precepts they previously received, they undergo the bodhisattva precepts; it is for this reason that such a statement is made. How is this known to be so? From the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*...

The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-viniścaya* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Because only those in the human realm are able to receive the bodhisattva precepts, they are all called 'those of the foremost purity.
This [purity] has three meanings: first, because those who receive and uphold the bodhisattva precepts permanently sever the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*);
second, because they possess both the practice of self-benefit and the practice of benefiting others; third, with respect to unsurpassed enlightenment..."
For this reason, those who uphold the precepts of the Two Vehicles merely sever the afflictive hindrances;
they practice solely for their own benefit and not for the benefit of others, and they look only toward the end of their physical life rather than toward unsurpassed bodhi.
Now, these Bodhisattva precepts possess three such superior qualities over the Two Vehicles, and are therefore called "foremost. As for what is termed "pure":
At that time, although they have not yet purified the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), they possess the bodhicitta that causes those two obstacles to be purified;

therefore, it is said they are "purified. The rest is as explained in the sūtra regarding the six types of spiritual lineages (*gotra*). Although Bodhisattvas possess both obstacles, they possess the bodhicitta that causes those two obstacles to be purified;
therefore, it is said they have "purified the two obstacles. The introductory section (*nidāna*) concludes here, as it was already presented previously.
The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddhas, beginning the second section, the "Section on the Correct Exposition. This section contains two parts: first, the elucidation of the ten grave precepts;
second, the elucidation of the forty-eight light precepts. Within the first part, there are three sub-sections: (1) a general explanation for beginners;

(2) a detailed interpretation of the prohibitions, beginning with "The Buddha told the sons of the Buddhas: 'If one kills oneself... and so forth; and (3) [the treatment] regarding those who have committed an offense.
Below: A summary of the re-enactment of the precepts. This section also consists of three parts: first, citing the number and indicating the names;
second, exhorting others to recite and study them; third, summarizing and exhorting study.

The second section, "Exhorting Others to Recite and Study," contains two parts: first, citing those who do not recite to exhort them; second, citing those who do recite to exhort them. Regarding the term "non-Bodhisattva":

it refers to one who has developed the intention not to recite the precepts. This designation as a "non-Bodhisattva" is made on account of their state of mind; it does not mean they are permanently no longer Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, even such a non-Bodhisattva can still practice with maturity, though they are said to lack the seed of Buddhahood; this does not mean they are permanently [without it].

Because they are not sons of the Buddha, they are not the seeds of the Buddha. One interpretation states: those who attain Buddhahood do so because they possess the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*);

since they have attained Buddhahood precisely by this, those who give rise to the unwholesome mind of not reciting the precepts do not possess such knowledge of all modes, and thus they lack the seed. Therefore, they are not the seed.
One who forms the intention not to recite the precepts commits a minor offense. However, there is no offense if one intends to engage in other superior activities;

or if, having already performed those activities, one subsequently recites the precepts; or if one has formed neither the intention to perform nor the intention not to recite, yet despite making an effort to recite, fails to do so due to dull faculties. For followers of the Hīnayāna, if they form the thought not to recite, [they commit an offense].
If one intentionally transgresses after that point, one incurs the offense of not training (*aśikṣā-āpatti*). If it is an offense committed through ignorance, one incurs it only after five years.
The remaining meanings are as stated above. Regarding what is called the tenfold *prātimokṣa*:
if one does not uphold these ten grave precepts, one cannot be called a *prātimokṣa*. If one is able to uphold them, there is the sense of being liberated from bondage.
Below this is the second section, the specific prohibitions for others. Within this, there are ten precepts, thus forming ten sections.

The first is the precept against killing; this is named according to the practice of restraint (*śīla*). It is also called the "precept of killing," which is named according to the transgression of commission.
The characteristics and the two types of names for the subsequent precepts may be understood by analogy with the above. Within this precept, there are three [parts].

Section. First, the Buddha tells the sons of the Buddha that there are those who possess the capacity [to receive the precepts], which indicates the essential nature [of the recipient]. Second, from "if one kills oneself" onwards, the various matters clarify the secondary transgressions (*anuvyañjana*).

Third, from "and if one [kills] oneself" onwards, it cites improper conduct to define the faults. Regarding the first point, "the Buddha tells the sons of the Buddha": these are words intended to strike the responsive faculty (*indriya*) of the listener.

This is because those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and the like do not possess the responsive faculty for hearing the Bodhisattva precepts, and thus they are not the ones for whom [the teaching] is intended. There is...
Since it is for the sake of the bodhisattva sons of the Buddha that the bodhisattva precepts are now being expounded, it says, "The Buddha addressed the sons of the Buddha.

Regarding the term "sons of the Buddha," this refers to the person to indicate the essence [of the precepts]; thus, it is said to "indicate the essence. From the section on "if one kills oneself" onwards, it clarifies the practice (anuvṛtti).
For example, in the Hīnayāna, the phrase "if a bhikṣu" indicates the essence of the recipient; from "common precepts" onwards...

The *Śīlaparivarta* (Chapter on Ethics) states that one becomes a bhikṣu only by possessing both the precept of undertaking (*samādāna-śīla*) and the precept of conformity (*anuvartana-śīla*). This principle is likewise applicable here:
one becomes a bodhisattva only by possessing both the sense of undertaking and the sense of conformity.
