The second section, "Listing the Matters," which clarifies the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), consists of two parts. The first part lists the prohibitions; the second, from "Furthermore, these are bodhisattvas... onwards, clarifies the correct practice as the antidote.

This section is also titled "Raising the Active Observance to Accomplish the Passive Observance. Within the first part (the listing of prohibitions), there are two sub-sections: first, the listing of grave prohibitions;
second, from "...down to all [other matters]" onwards, the listing of minor prohibitions. Within the former (the grave prohibitions), there are likewise two parts.
First, the correct [view] and its refutations are set forth; subsequently, the completion of karma through the requisite conditions is explained.

Within the explanation of the refutations, first, with reference to the three grades of sentient beings, the gradations of the lightness or heaviness of their offenses, as well as the commonality of their loss regarding magnitude, are manifested.
Following this, the meaning of taking life is explained. First, regarding sentient beings of the superior grade: these are parents, determined Bodhisattvas, and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The Sage [states]: "If one kills such a superior person, one commits two grave obstructive offenses (*ānantarya*).

Regarding the results for those of inferior [capacity], the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* contains two different passages, one superior and one inferior. If one follows the superior passage, Jīvaka says to King Ajātaśatru:
"You have committed two heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), namely, killing a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and killing your father. If one follows the inferior passage, it is only...

Taking the fruit of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) constitutes a transgression against the Buddha, because one does not take the three lower fruits. Regarding those of "intermediate capacity" (*madhyama-bhāga*): this refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) on the path.
Killing such a person of intermediate capacity constitutes only a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), but not a transgression against the Buddha.

As for taking gods as being of intermediate capacity, this is based on the Mahāyāna perspective; if based on the Hīnayāna, killing a god constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense. Those of "inferior capacity" (*mṛdu-bhāga*) are non-humans and animals.
Regarding the killing of those of inferior grade: one commits only a light secondary offense (*āpatti*), not a grave offense.
If one kills a human being who holds wrong views, for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dìdì Qiǎnjī, there is no fault, but only merit. If it is a novice Bodhisattva, they commit a light secondary offense.
If it is a follower of the Hīnayāna, killing a human being constitutes a grave offense; killing a deva or a non-human (*amanuṣya*) constitutes an offense of the third category.
One who kills an animal commits an offense under the sixth category.

Second, regarding the clarification of severing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), there are differences among the three assemblies. According to the Sarvāstivāda school, it is distinct from the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
There exists a life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) that is neither form nor mind. When one refutes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one simultaneously refutes that life-faculty;

therefore, one commits the transgression of the precept against killing. According to the Satyasiddhi school, the life-faculty consists of the continuity of form and mind, with karma from previous lives serving as its root.
Because one causes this continuity of form and mind to be severed, one commits the transgression of the precept against killing. In this school’s view, within the continuity of form and mind...
Although the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is provisionally established, there is no separate ontological essence of a life-faculty apart from form and mind.

Regarding this, those of the Mahāyāna have three explanations: first, that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) constitutes the life-faculty; second, that the ālayavijñāna constitutes the life-faculty; and third, that...
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is provisionally established within the various states of the ālayavijñāna.
Regarding the latter two explanations, if one follows the general approach, the first is preferable; if one considers the specific approach, the latter is also acceptable.

From the perspective of the specific approach, although it is not the life-faculty as defined by the Sarvāstivādins—which is not a real entity distinct from mind—it is nonetheless a life-faculty that is neither matter nor mind, based upon the ālayavijñāna.
Regarding the Dharma: because that which is conventionally designated is not non-existent, one can sever this conventionally designated life; therefore, one commits the precept against killing.

This does not depend on severing the *ālaya-vijñāna*; thus, it constitutes the offense of killing. Since the *ālaya-vijñāna* is an indestructible dharma, there are five propositions concerning self-killing that establish the gravity or lightness of the offense, as well as the similarities and differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Namely, the first is when one treats a human being as a human being—[this applies to both] Mahāyāna and [Hīnayāna].
Because the object and the mental state share the same focal point. Second is the doubt regarding whether [the object] is a human or a non-human.
If one follows the Hīnayāna, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that it constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*), whereas the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.

The commentary explains: the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* is based on the sense of doubting whether the object is a human; the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is based on the sense of doubting whether the object is a non-human. If one approaches both types of objects indiscriminately...

Regarding the doubts concerning the middle [category]: one incurs two grave offenses. For a Mahāyāna practitioner, it constitutes a grave offense. Third, if a person is perceived as a non-human being:
according to the Hīnayāna, if this refers to a shift in perception, the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) constitutes an offense of the third category (*sthūlātyaya*);

the subsequent mind, because it is the preliminary effort for killing a non-human, is a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). If it concerns a Mahāyāna practitioner, both the preceding and succeeding minds constitute a light defilement offense (*pāyantika*). If, however, [it concerns]...

Regarding those who are fundamentally deluded: if from beginning to end they do not commit murder, then for one whose mind is like a block of wood—deluded—the offense is entirely absent, whether the act be great or small, because they are deluded regarding what is not an object of transgression. As for one deluded such that their mind is like a block of wood, this is an innate delusion;

it is not a delusion acquired through learning, for it is not known through study. Even if one is fundamentally deluded, if they are deluded regarding non-humans or animals [in place of humans], [the same principle applies].
Because one is deluded regarding the object of the transgression: for a follower of the Hīnayāna, the preparatory act of killing a non-human or an animal constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (misdeed).
For a follower of the Mahāyāna, it constitutes a minor offense (*laghu-mala-pāpa*). Fourth, if one perceives a non-human as a human:

for a follower of the Hīnayāna, this constitutes an offense of the third category (*tṛtīya-skandha*) because it is a preparatory act of killing a human. For a follower of the Mahāyāna, it constitutes a minor offense. Fifth, if one suspects a non-human to be a human.
In the Hīnayāna, if the doubt concerns a human being belonging to one of the five destinies, one commits an offense of the third category;
if the doubt concerns a non-human being belonging to one of the five destinies, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). In the Mahāyāna, this constitutes a light defiling offense (*mṛdumrakṣa*).
Regarding "teaching others to kill": in the Hīnayāna, if one teaches another person to kill for one's own sake, one certainly commits a grave offense (pārājika).

If one teaches another to kill a person on behalf of you, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*. Although there is no explicit textual authority for this, it may be so inferred by analogy with the precept against stealing.

Question: Among the three types of *sthūlātyaya*, which one is this? Answer: Teaching another to kill a human being constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. If one instructs [another] regarding the realm of non-humans...

Regarding "causing another to kill": it refers to instructing another to kill an animal; this constitutes a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). As for this act of instructing another to kill, in the Mahāyāna, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of another, all constitute a grave offense (*pārājika*).
If one instructs another while in a state of mind characterized by any of the three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna agree that it is a grave offense.
Regarding the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of killing—such as administering medicine to cause an abortion to kill the fetus, or providing lethal drugs to be consumed—the same applies.
There are three ways in which one praises the act of killing. First, seeing a person who practices virtue, one says: "It would be better for you to die quickly while practicing virtue.
If you live long, will you not create mental karma through thoughts of resentment and malicious intent? Hearing these words, that person dies immediately.
Second, seeing a person who has committed mental karma, one says: "It would be better for you to die quickly while your transgression is still small. If...
Regarding those who have lived for a long time: because they can produce even more mental karma (*manas-karman*), there are three [reasons].

Third, when they hear the words of an old person or a sick person saying, "It would be better to die quickly and be free from suffering than to endure this long life and long suffering," those people hear these three words and consequently die.
The one who praises [the act] commits a grave offense; both the great and the small are equally guilty. As for the one who rejoices upon seeing it being done:
because they rejoice upon seeing someone kill, and because that person sees their joyful mind and thus performs the karmic act of killing, the one who rejoices commits a grave offense.
This is as stated in the Vinaya: When the Tathāgata was teaching the contemplation of impurity to the assembly of bhikṣus on the banks of the Kauśika River...
Because we, such as Kāśyapa and others, have practiced this contemplation, we have severed the true body and mind.
At that time, one bhikṣu said to the bhikṣu Muḷika, "I give my robes and bowl to you, for you have killed me. That bhikṣu Muḷika then killed him.
Having finished killing him, he went to the riverbank; while he was washing his knife, Māra appeared in the middle of the river and expressed his sympathetic joy.
[The Buddha] spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent! You, O bhikṣu, are able to deliver those who have not yet been delivered.
When the bhikṣu heard these words, he naturally took them as a meritorious deed. He went to where the other bhikṣus were and said, "Those who have not yet been delivered are coming;
I shall now deliver them. At that time, those who had not yet abandoned desire died, while those bhikṣus who had already abandoned desire all [remained].
He wished to die. Thus, the bhikṣu Mulika killed sixty bhikṣus because they had gathered for a small assembly on the day of the poṣadha.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked: "Why is the assembly so small today? The other bhikṣus explained:
"The bhikṣu Mulika has killed them, which is why there are so few. This Mulika was one who delighted in killing by means of Māra.
Therefore, taking such [states] as rejoicing in killing constitutes a *dhāraṇī-sūtra*. It says: "This rejoicing in killing is the sixth grave precept (*guruka-śīla*).
If one rejoices after the death has already occurred, in the Mahāyāna this constitutes a minor defilement offense (*laghu-mala-apatti*); for those of the Hīnayāna, it is a transgression (*duṣkṛta*).
The phrase "and so forth" includes killing out of anger. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Because of the arousal of a mind of anger by a rishi..."

He protected this seer by raining down stones from his sleeves to extinguish [the fire]. Regarding the aforementioned [deities] such as those of the Magadha kingdom, these clarify the "killing of the body.

This "killing through anger" refers to the killing of the mental karma (*manas-karma*). As for the "killing through incantations" mentioned below, this refers to the killing of the vocal karma (*vāk-karma*).
It is called "killing" because among the spirits there are those who can be incanted; those spirits go forth to kill people, and they can also be incanted to cause corpses to seize swords. He...

Regarding the items such as "a corpse going to kill a person" and so forth: the above does not constitute nine distinct categories, because within the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of killing there are three types.

These nine [categories] applied to the three grades of sentient beings result in twenty-seven precepts. If one considers the objects to be killed, since all sentient beings are immeasurable, the precepts are likewise immeasurable.
This concludes the formal enumeration of the non-characteristics (*avijñapti*).

Below the section on the karma of killing, the second part clarifies the karma of the precept regarding the fulfillment of conditions. Within this precept, if five conditions are met, the full karma is established.

First is the objective field (*viṣaya*): if the object belongs to the realm of non-humans or similar beings, there is a minor offense (*āpatti*). Second is the perception of the person (*puruṣa-saṃjñā*).
Even when approaching human habitations, if one perceives them as non-humans and so forth, it constitutes a minor offense of defilement. Third, regarding the arousal of the intent to kill:

this means that if one does not arouse the intent to kill from beginning to end, yet shoots at a mountain non-human being or the like because one is unaware of its presence—even though there was no intent to kill—if one mistakenly strikes and kills a heavy object or a living being, there is no offense whatsoever. Fourth...
This refers to the arousal of skillful means (*upāya*). If one does not arouse skillful means, it is a minor defilement (*laghu-pāpaka*). Question:

If the preceding intentional state and other conditions are fully present, yet at the moment of killing there is no conscious intent—due to error or the like—what offense is committed? Answer: According to the Hīnayāna, this belongs to the third category of offenses;
according to the Mahāyāna, it constitutes a minor defilement. Fifth: severing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). If one does not sever the life-faculty, [it is not a grave offense].

Because it is a light offense (*āpatti*). Among the five conditions, the first two serve as the conditions (*pratyaya*); the third serves as the cause (*hetu*); the fourth serves as the action (*karma*);
and the fifth serves as the factor (*dharma*). The Commentary (*Śāstra*) states: "Taking the instruments of killing, such as swords and staves, as the factor.

However, this does not accord with the meaning, for one can effect a killing even in the absence of instruments such as swords and staves. Therefore, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is taken as [the factor].
Regarding the Dharma: if there is no sentient being (life-faculty), the karma of killing is not established. Therefore, among the five conditions, if the cause is missing, there is no offense at all;
if any of the conditions are missing, or if they are mutually deficient, one incurs a minor defilement offense (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*).

The phrase "and so forth" includes the minor defilement offense of killing animals; thus it says "and so forth. The prohibition against intentional killing is intended to distinguish this from accidental killing.
Therefore, it is called "intentional killing. If one kills by mistake without intent, there is only the karmic path [of action], but no offense of violating the precepts.

For this reason, the following passage presents the accomplishment of "observance through cessation" (śīla-saṃvara) based on "active practice" (pravṛtti): namely, for one who constantly practices and cultivates a mind of compassion.
Because by performing the observance of action (*kriyā-śīla*), one accomplishes the observance of restraint (*vāraṇa-śīla*) through the precept against killing;

or because by means of the observance of restraint, one accomplishes the observance of action, such as when one intends to perform the *poṣadha* or other such rites, being able to first cease all other activities and exclude those such as novices (*śrāmaṇera*) due to the existence of other rules of conduct.
Or, by committing an offense of action, one incurs an offense of restraint, namely, by violating the rule regarding [the failure to] recite [the scriptures].

Regarding the time of observing the precepts: one should not recite them merely to emulate others, for one must first master the precepts themselves. Furthermore, there are cases where the observance of prohibitions (*śīla-saṃvara*) results in the commission of an offense;
this refers to when people today engage in the act of taking life, yet do not openly appear as monks (*bhikṣu*) and so forth.

Within these precepts, it is shown that the practice of active observance (*vidhi-ācaraṇa*) constitutes the observance of prohibitions. How could there be no clear meaning regarding the practice of virtuous conduct? This is for the purpose of encompassing all wholesome qualities.

Regarding the Dharma-precepts: since all ten grave precepts are *saṃvara-śīla* (restraint-precepts), within the precepts for the lower assemblies (*hīna-saṃgha*), there are cases where one is cited for maintaining *vṛtti-śīla* (conduct) and thereby accomplishes *kriyā-śīla* (action-precepts);
there are also cases where one is cited for maintaining *kriyā-śīla* and thereby accomplishes *vṛtti-śīla*.

Furthermore, there are cases where one is cited for committing a transgression of *kriyā-śīla* and thereby accomplishes *vṛtti-śīla*, or cases where one is cited for committing a transgression of *vṛtti-śīla* and thereby accomplishes *kriyā-śīla*. It cannot be said that these are merely *saṃvara-śīla*.
Because there is the undertaking and maintaining [of precepts], it constitutes the morality of gathering correct Dharma (*saddharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

Even up to the point of undertaking and maintaining deportment and conduct, the morality of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) is taken as the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*). Nevertheless, each individual precept follows wherever one goes.

That which explains and penetrates compassion is called the morality of gathering sentient beings (*sattva-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). What is meant by "following the practice of filial piety"? It refers to the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*). What is meant by "following the practice that accords with the mind"?

This refers to the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*śīla-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*). Regarding "practicing according to skillful means," this refers to practices such as the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*).

"Rescuer" means rescuing others so that they are freed from suffering; thus one is called a "protector. Furthermore, because one protects and attends to them so that they may obtain benefit, one is called a "guardian of their self-will."
"What is meant by 'resolute intention' (adhyāśaya) arising fervently from within the mind? It is not merely that a resolute intention arises from within the mind;

it can also manifest that resolute intention such that there is no fear or doubt. Therefore, it is called 'resolute intention. As for *pārājika*, although its translated name includes 'falling' (*patana*),"

It is not as [significant] as the many names such as "severing the head" and so forth; rather, the meaning of "the ultimate sense" (*atyanta-artha*) clarified in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* should be understood according to this scriptural passage.
That Vinaya states: "The ultimate sense has three meanings. The first is 'receding' (*parihāṇi*), which refers to one who violates this precept."
Because there are no divisions within the fruit of the Way (*mārgaphala*). This meaning corresponds to what is stated in the following passage:

"If one commits an offense, one shall not be able to give rise to the bodhicitta in this present body, nor attain the ten stages of departure (*niryāṇa*), the ten stages of nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the ten adamantine stages (*vajra*), the ten stages (*bhūmi*), or the wondrous fruit of the ever-abiding Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Second, regarding "not dwelling together": this means that if one violates this precept, one may not participate in the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) or the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and so forth.
Within the two types of *karmavācanā*, one cannot be counted as a member of the Saṃgha.
This principle applies even to those who, having committed an offense, lose their status as a king or a *cakravartin*, and lose their status as a *bhikṣu* or *bhikṣuṇī*.
Third is what is called "falling" (*pātayantikā*); that is to say, if one violates this precept, after casting off the body, one will fall into the Avīci Hell.

Therefore, this meaning is as stated below: "If there is one who commits an offense, they shall fall into the three evil realms for two or three kalpas, not hearing the names of their parents or the Triple Gem.
Within this precept, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are established to briefly distinguish between observance and violation.
First, there are cases where one kills a person yet it is exclusively merit rather than sin. This refers to Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over the turning of the wheel [of destiny].
Because they can discern the capacities of beings, they may kill those whose capacities are such that they cannot be saved; for such killing is exclusively merit and not sin. As the sutra says:
Although one may kill five hundred brāhmaṇas, there is no offense; one merely incurs [the result of] "gathering" (saṃgraha) and so forth.

Second, there are cases where killing a person constitutes neither an offense nor merit—namely, killing through error or delusion—and so forth. This is because there is only the path of karma (karmapatha), and no offense of violating the precepts.
Third, there are cases where it is only light and not heavy; that is, within this precept, the killing of sentient beings of inferior grade is also established as such.
Fourth, it is exclusively grave and not light. That is to say, among the four propositions established for these fundamental precepts:
the first proposition is exclusively merit and not transgression; the second is neither transgression nor merit; and the latter two are exclusively transgression and not merit.
The second precept against stealing, also known as the precept of non-stealing. The reason for its designation may be understood by analogy with the preceding [precepts].

Within this section, there are three parts: first, citing the person to indicate the essence [of the offense]; second, enumerating the objects to clarify the principle; third, citing what is improper to conclude the fault.
This section is also titled "Citing Improper Conduct to Conclude the Offense. Its status as a minor section is no different from that of the preceding precepts. What follows...

Regarding theft, it shall be categorized according to the three types of owners' property, clarifying the gravity of the offenses and the similarities and differences between their magnitudes. The three types of owners' property are:

first, the property of the Triple Gem; second, the property of human beings; and third, the property of non-human beings. Within this, the doctrine of the Hīnayāna will be clarified first, followed by an analysis of the property of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the property of the Triple Gem: as for stealing the property of the Buddha, one does not incur the full offense of theft with respect to the Buddha himself, because the Buddha has no notion of "I" or "mine" regarding objects and harbors no intent to harm them;
therefore, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* (light offense). This is because such property is categorized as belonging to non-human entities. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"When constructing a Buddhist temple, using pearls, flowers, and the like for offerings is different from taking them [by force] for one's own use. If one knows this...
Know that all such acts constitute a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If there is a guardian or owner, one incurs a grave offense (*pārājika*) in relation to the property of the Triple Gem.
If there is no guardian, one incurs an offense in relation to severing the merit of the original donor. Therefore, the *Vinaya-nidāna* states:

"If one steals banners, canopies, or other items from a stupa of the Buddha or a stupa of a Śrāvaka, one incurs an offense in relation to severing the merit of the original donor. Thus, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* says: "Stealing..."
Regarding the Buddha’s precious objects and the ritual implements within the vihāra: if a guardian appraises their value, it constitutes an offense.

However, if one steals them with the intention that they be used for the Buddha’s successors and so forth, there is no offense, as the items will certainly be stolen for the purpose of making offerings. The Sarvāstivādins state that because one steals for the sake of the Buddha, there is no offense.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is said that stealing relics for the purpose of pure-hearted offering is likewise permissible; one makes a vow, saying: "He was my teacher, and I am his teacher."

Regarding this intention: it is not a violation of the *Mātṛkā* to say that stealing the Buddha’s post-cremation relics (*śarīra*) when they do not amount to five *māṣaka* is a *sthūlātyaya*, whereas stealing them when they amount to five constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). Next, regarding the theft of the Dharma: the Dharma is insentient and lacks the notion of "mine.

That the Vinaya prescribes a grave offense for its theft is based on the presence of a guardian who possesses such a sense of ownership. The text states: "At one time, there was a bhikṣu who stole another's scripture..."

The calculation of paper and ink involves a heavy burden, whereas the Buddha’s words are priceless. Therefore, according to the *Śāriputra-mūla-vinaya-mātṛkā* and the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya*, one incurs a grave offense (*pārājika*) when the value of the expected reward from the owner reaches five *māṣaka*.

Regarding the theft of a scripture, the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that if the calculated value of the paper and ink reaches five *māṣaka*, and the labor involved is complete, one commits a grave offense.
The *Mātṛkā* says: "If the value of the stolen scriptural object reaches five *māṣaka*, one incurs a grave offense; if it does not reach it, one commits a light offense. Thus says Master Fayuan.
The text says: This treatise states that those who steal the scriptures are equivalent to those who steal from the Buddha; subsequently, one who steals out of a spirit of malice commits an offense.
However, the owner of the money takes only the text regarding the commission of the offense, not the original text concerning the root offense.

Next, regarding the theft of monastic property (*saṃghika-vastu*), if there is a protector or owner, it is treated as a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) as described above. Furthermore, there are four types of monastic property: first, permanent property (*nitya-sthāvara*). "Permanent" means...

The kitchen, storehouses, temple buildings, communal utensils, flower and fruit trees, groves, fields, gardens, servants, livestock, and so forth, have a substance that pervades the ten directions and thus cannot be divided for individual use;

they belong collectively to the Sangha as a whole, like a single heavy object. Second, there are those things permanently established for the ten directions, such as the regular food provided to the monastic community;
while their substance pervades the ten directions, they are restricted solely to the specific assembly in question. If there is someone who protects the temple...
Regarding the owner: if one expects the owner to incur a grave offense, yet steals and causes damage in common with others, one should be subject to a light offense. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If one takes the surplus food of the Saṃgha or obstructs a dwelling, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* states: "If one takes property belonging to the Saṃgha as if it were one's own and uses it or gives it away, it is the same as a *sthūlātyaya*.
Taking it with a thieving mind—regardless of the amount—is what constitutes an offense; this is called the fifth great thief. (End of excerpt)
The *Jianyun* states: "To eat monastic food without having struck the bell constitutes the offense of theft. Third is "the present before one's eyes" (*xiànqián*).

If one steals this object, the gravity of the offense is determined with respect to the original owner. If many people share an object and one person guards it, the offense is likewise determined with respect to that guardian.
Fourth is "the present throughout the ten directions," such as the light articles belonging to the five groups of renunciants. The *Shansheng jing* states: "Stealing what has been lost..."
Regarding the property of the bhikṣu-saṃgha: if the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has not yet been performed, one incurs an offense against the Saṃgha of the ten directions;

this is considered light, meaning that if the number of people is less than five, one commits only a *sthūlātyaya* offense. If the ritual has already been performed, the offense is incurred with respect to the present Saṃgha and is grave;

this means that when the number of people is fixed and sufficient to reach five, it is a grave offense. Furthermore, the mutual use of the property of the Three Jewels and other such matters are as explained in detail in the *Guangchao*. Second:

If one steals human property, stealing five *kārsāpaṇa* or more constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*); stealing less than five constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*. Third, there are three types of stealing non-human property:
first, stealing from humans [as defined above] is a *sthūlātyaya*; second, stealing from spirits or deities is also a *sthūlātyaya*; third, stealing the property of animals:
if one steals the remains of a lion, there is no offense, because there is no sense of ownership or attachment; as for other animals...
Living beings are all auspicious. If there is a protector, one commits a grave offense.
Regarding the clarification of Mahāyāna principles hereafter: among the various objects previously explained, if they constitute a grave offense in the Hīnayāna, one likewise incurs a grave offense;
if they constitute a minor offense in the Hīnayāna, one incurs a light defilement offense. This is because the training in the precepts is the same. From [here]...

Regarding theft, there are five analytical cases. First: when there is an owner and one perceives it as having an owner, the offense is grave regardless of the value, because the object and the mental state correspond.

Second: when there is doubt regarding whether an object has an owner or not; according to the Mahāsāṃghika of the Hīnayāna, this is grave, whereas according to the Dharmaguptaka, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

In the Mahāyāna, this is grave. Third, regarding an object with an owner, one perceives it as having no owner: in the Hīnayāna, such a shift in perception incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; in the Mahāyāna, it is a minor defiling offense (*āpatti*).
If there was fundamental delusion [regarding ownership], both vehicles consider it non-offensive. Fourth, regarding an object with no owner, one perceives it as having an owner:
in the Hīnayāna, this is a *sthūlātyaya*; in the Mahāyāna, one incurs a minor defiling offense. Fifth, regarding an object with no owner, one suspects it has an owner.

In the Hīnayāna, this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*; in the Mahāyāna, it is a light offense. Regarding those who instruct others to steal: in the Hīnayāna, if one instructs another, saying "Steal for you," one commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one says "Steal for me" or "Steal for you," and the value reaches five *māṣakas*, one commits a grave offense (*pārājika*); if it does not reach five, one commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
In the Mahāyāna, if one instructs another, whether saying "for me" or "for you," one commits a grave offense in both cases. Regarding preparatory acts of theft: stealing from empty consciousness.

...and so forth. Because one dares to act [thus], purchasing land that another cherishes, planting trees on another's land, or building houses there, thereby causing that person to lose the prior use of their land and so on, it is said that one commits "theft of empty consciousness.

If there is an artisan who intends to grant instruction only after being given to the Sangha, yet through a stratagem falsely claims to have given them to the Sangha, and having already learned the craft, does not pay the price, he steals from that person.

Human intelligence. Therefore, the valuation determines the offense; whether large or small, the regulation is the same. To clarify the formation of the karmic action through its constituent conditions: when six conditions are fulfilled, the full karmic action is established. First is the object, which is a person or thing.
This means that stealing the property of a non-human being or an animal constitutes a minor offense. Second is the perception of the object as a person or thing;
this means that one who steals while perceiving it as the property of a non-human being or the like incurs a minor offense. Third is the arousal of the intent to steal.
If one does not give rise to the thought of theft from beginning to end, there is no offense. Fourth, regarding "valuable objects": if it is less than five [units], one incurs a minor offense.

Fifth, regarding "initiating or not initiating the preparatory effort": this constitutes a minor defiled offense (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*). Sixth, regarding "moving from its original location or not moving from its original location":
if one does not move it from its original location, it is a minor defiled offense in accordance with the preparatory effort; thus, what would have been a full offense is rendered incomplete.
Therefore, among these, the first two serve as conditions; the fourth, the heavy object, serves as the phenomenon; the sixth, the removal from its original place, serves as the factor;

the third, the arousal of the intent to steal, serves as the cause; and the fifth, the undertaking of the preparatory effort, serves as the action. If the cause is lacking, there is no offense at all.
Each and every one constitutes a light offense of defilement. Regarding "stealing by incantation": this refers to taking another's property through the use of spells.

As for the question concerning "five coins," what amount does this correspond to according to the currency of this country? The answer is: it is based on five large copper coins. If small coins are used, sixteen of them equal one large coin;
thus, five times six (of the small coins) equals thirty, which totals eighty small coins. Therefore, it is eighty small coins.
"According to this country's standard, five coins (pañca-kārṣāpaṇa) corresponds to eight bushels of rice. However, regarding the theft of heavy objects, there should be four permutations:
first, there is the case where one steals five coins and it constitutes a grave offense, meaning one steals five coins at a time when they are neither expensive nor cheap;
second, there is the case where one steals five coins but it is light and not grave, meaning one steals them at a time when they are cheap; third, there is the case where one steals five coins..."
It is grave, not light. This refers to stealing money at a time when it is of high value. Fourth, there is the case where one steals five coins but they are insufficient;

thus the offense is light, not grave. This refers to actually stealing items of little value. The phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) is used to encompass the broader category of minor offenses involving the theft of grass, wood, and so forth;
hence the use of "up to. It is also used to extend broadly from human property to the property of spirits and deities; hence the use of "up to."

Regarding "ghosts and spirits" (*bhūta* and *deva*): one interpretation states that those among humans are called ghosts (*preta*), while those among the heavens are called spirits (*deva*). Another interpretation states that those who are sycophantic, crooked, and restless are called ghosts;
those who possess inconceivable, hidden arts are called spirits. As for one who presides over the property of a thief:

if that person subsequently seizes back the goods after they have been taken, it is because the thief is seizing from another thief. Therefore, in calculating the value of the money, if one can seize it from the person [who took it], the offense constitutes a grave transgression (*pārājika*), regardless of whether the amount is large or small.

The same rule applies. "Not stealing intentionally" means that there is no offense for taking what is mistakenly thought to be one's own property, taking what is perceived as ownerless property, or taking the property of a friend or relative;
therefore, it specifies "intentional stealing. As for the statement that "one should give rise to the Buddha-nature," this is because sentient beings are themselves the Buddha-nature.
A sutra says: "The Dharma-realm circulates through the five realms of existence; therefore, they are called 'sentient beings' (sattva). Thus, regarding...
Within this, four propositions are established to distinguish between upholding and violating [the precept]. First, although one steals five coins, there is merit rather than transgression;

this refers to a Bodhisattva who has mastered the mechanism of the wheel [of means], and thus steals an object because it can be used to save a sentient being. Second, although one steals, there is neither transgression nor merit;
this refers to the explanation regarding taking what belongs to no owner, and so forth. Third, it is merely light and not grave; this refers to this particular precept.
Furthermore, this includes the minor offenses of stealing grass, wood, or divine objects. Fourth, there are those that are exclusively grave and not minor;
these refer to the grave precepts established within this very section of the precepts. Among these four phrases: the first phrase refers to merit alone and not to offense;
the second phrase refers to neither merit nor offense; and the final two phrases refer exclusively to offense and not to merit.
The third is the precept against sexual misconduct, also known as the precept of celibacy. It is studied by all members of the five assemblies, both great and small.

Within it, there are three sections: first, citing the person to indicate the essence; second, citing what is prohibited to clarify the teaching; and third, citing what is prohibited to conclude with the transgression.

In the middle section, there are two parts: first, the formal enumeration of what is prohibited; second, the clarification of the teaching beginning with "A bodhisattva should... Within the enumeration of what is prohibited, there is also...

There are two parts: first, the enumeration of grave offenses; second, the enumeration of light offenses. Within the first [section], there are also two: first, the formal enumeration of the offenses; second, the clarification of how the factors combine to constitute the karma.

Regarding the first [category], sexual misconduct, five propositions are established: 1. A legitimate path with the perception of it being a legitimate path—whether involving the large or small [orifices], this is equally grave. 2.

A legitimate path with doubt as to whether it is a legitimate path or not—whether involving the large or small [orifices], this is equally grave. 3. A legitimate path with the perception of it being a non-legitimate path... [text continues]

Regarding the perception [of the object]: the gravity [of the offense] is the same regardless of size. As for why other precepts—specifically the third phrase—are considered light offenses, whereas this precept is universally considered grave:
if one considers it from the perspective of the path of karma (*karmapatha*), it is lighter than the precept against killing.

However, because sexual misconduct is the root from which all transgressions arise and constitutes an extreme fault, it is strictly prohibited. Within the three phrases of the Right Path, those who engage in sexual misconduct are all...

[The first three] are grave. Fourth, regarding what is not the Path, one perceives it as the Path: this is the third category for the Hīnayāna, while it constitutes a light defilement for the Mahāyāna. Fifth, regarding what is not the Path, one has doubt about it:
this is the third category for the Hīnayāna, while it constitutes a transgression of a light degree for the Mahāyāna. As for teaching others to engage in sexual misconduct:

if one follows the Hīnayāna, where self-benefit is primary, then teaching others to engage in sexual misconduct does not mean that one’s own practice is free from defilement; therefore, it constitutes a transgression of the third category.
If there is mutual communication between this person and that person, it constitutes the second category [of offense]. In the Mahāyāna, altruistic conduct is primary;
therefore, although one may personally remain untainted among human beings, the meaning of defiling another is extremely grave, and thus the offense is equally a heavy transgression.
How much more so in the case of acting as a matchmaker! As for the phrase "even unto all women," although they are all appropriate objects, the reference is specifically to human women.

It extends to animals and so forth; therefore, it says "up to and including. It says "all" with reference to the renunciant bodhisattva, meaning that because the renunciant bodhisattva has severed both the correct and the improper types of sexual misconduct, there are no women who are not improper or grave objects [of such conduct];
hence, it says "all. Among women, there are three paths: namely, the large path (the anus), the small path (the vagina), and the mouth. Among the gods, there are two paths: namely, the large path...

Practicing [the path] through both body and speech constitutes the sixfold gravity of the object (*viṣaya*). Regarding the statement "one must not intentionally engage in sexual misconduct": this is to distinguish cases where one is coerced by an enemy;

if one comes into contact with the object but does not experience the three moments [of arousal], or if it occurs during sleep, or if another person commits the act on one's behalf, there is no offense from beginning to end.
Therefore, it is said that one must not intentionally engage in sexual misconduct. As for the statement regarding the "complete conditions," the four conditions bring about its fulfillment.
Regarding the karma: first, it is the correct path; for if one acts upon an improper object, it constitutes a minor offense. Second, there is the presence of a defiled mind;

however, if one is coerced by an enemy and, despite being in contact with the object, lacks a defiled mind throughout the three times [of preparation, execution, and completion], there is no offense at all.
Third, the initiation of the means; fourth, causing the object not to meet with the object, which is a minor offense. Among these, the first serves as the causal condition.
Next is the object; third is the action; fourth is the phenomenon. If a condition is missing, it is light and not grave; if the cause is missing, there is no offense at all.

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between light and grave based on the correct path: violating a human female is grave, whereas violating a female animal and so forth constitutes a light karmic path.
Also, when discussing this in terms of the human realm: violating one who has left the household life is grave, while violating [a laywoman]... [is light].
For those living as householders, there is a distinction between what is light and what is heavy; the same applies to upholding or violating the precepts.
The subsequent statement, "down to sexual intercourse with female animals and through improper orifices," is made specifically regarding the householder bodhisattva.

This means that if a householder bodhisattva does not abandon sexual misconduct, even though it may involve improper orifices, it is nonetheless equivalent to sexual misconduct. However, regarding sexual misconduct, there is...
There are two kinds: first, sexual misconduct because it is not the [proper] way; second, sexual misconduct because it is not the [proper] part.
Regarding the former, it is also said that even if one commits an act within one's own sphere, if one engages in sexual intercourse in an improper manner, it is because it is unreasonable.

Second, [sexual misconduct] because it is not the [proper] place; that is to say, if it is at a stūpa or monastery where the Three Jewels reside, or beside one’s parents, or within the light of the sun or moon.

First, those such as the side of the preceptor; second, because of the improper time, namely the six monthly fast days, the three mid-months of the year, the period of pregnancy, the month following the birth of a child, and the time when menstrual blood flows;

third, because of protection by the Dharma, namely when one has violated the observance of the one-day precepts (*upavāsa*); and fourth, because of the improper path, namely excluding the usual minor paths and violating the four great [precepts].

Regarding the practice of the path and so forth, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states: "Even though she has not yet left her husband's household, because one commits sexual misconduct with her maidservant by way other than the [proper] path, one incurs the offense of illicit sexual conduct (*kāmamithyācāra*) and the like.

Although all four of these offenses are transgressions that are not light, they are considered heavy defiled offenses (*pāyattika*) because they involve violating what belongs to oneself rather than what belongs to another.
Within the latter category, there are also three types: first, those protected by the Dharma; this refers to violating a woman who has...

First, regarding the five classes of relatives and those who have received the precepts for leaving the household life; second, regarding protection by others, meaning because one is protected by one's mother or husband;
third, regarding those of a different species, meaning committing [sexual misconduct] with non-humans, animals, and so forth. Thus, the Fangdeng Tuoluoni Jing (Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra) states:
"Committing [misconduct] with birds or beasts constitutes sexual misconduct. These three cases do not depend on whether the path is right or wrong; they all constitute a grave offense.
Regarding the precepts: because [sexual misconduct] is not part of one's [proper] lot. Question: For what reason does a lay bodhisattva not abandon "right sexual conduct" (brahmacarya)?
Answer: The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states: "If one acquires property, one shall divide it into four parts: one part is given to parents, wife, and children;

one part is used for trade; and two parts are set aside for accumulation. Thus we know that he possesses his own wife. Furthermore, the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Renwang jing) states that a Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin) possesses...
Because of having a hundred sons or a thousand sons, a Wheel-Turning King [is compared to] a Bodhisattva from the first stage up to the tenth stage.

Therefore, one should know that regarding the Bodhisattvas who are householders, there are two ways in which they do not abandon sexual misconduct: First, they regard the minor path as the correct path;
though their speech is grand, they engage in the two paths [of sexual misconduct], which constitutes non-path. Second, they regard the three paths [of sexual misconduct] as the correct path. By...
Other body parts constitute non-ways, because committing sexual misconduct through improper ways is a transgression.

If one considers the case of renunciant bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and others, they all commit a grave offense by using the three [sexual] organs as the proper way; using other body parts constitutes a light offense.
If it is said that for a lay bodhisattva, acting through a non-way is considered deviant, this does not mean using other body parts.
It constitutes an improper path. Since both the mouth and the two [sexual] organs are improper paths, it is called sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*).

Regarding the "six relatives" (*ṣaḍ-bandhu*): these include the high ancestor and so forth; because the fourth ancestor is both father and son, they constitute six. It is the same for the maternal line.

If descendants are born from the fourth ancestor on either side, they are all considered six relatives. Within this context, four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established to distinguish between what is prohibited and what is permitted. First:

There are those who, although they commit sexual misconduct, possess exclusively merit and no fault. This refers to Bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī who have attained mastery over their spiritual capacities (*tathāgatagarbha*);
thus, for those who are to be saved by appearing in the form of a lustful man, they manifest the bodies of lustful men and lustful women in order to bring them across.
This is explained in detail in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*. Such is not the case for [ordinary] Mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, because there is nothing that is not so, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, in the "Buddha-dharma" chapter, states:

"If a bodhisattva practices what is not the path, it is because that bodhisattva has attained penetration into the Buddha-path. Second, there are also cases where one commits sexual misconduct yet incurs neither sin nor merit.

These include instances involving a deranged mind, a distracted mind, or a distressed mind; cases where one does not consent; or when the act is committed by another against oneself, or when one is coerced by an enemy—provided these occur during the three periods [of the day].

1. Not receiving pleasure and so forth, even if one consents to the mother’s confusion; 2. cases such as Ānanda’s commission of sexual misconduct and the like—these three are exclusively minor offenses and therefore not grave;
that is to say, when an ordained bodhisattva commits an offense involving a minor part of the body and so forth, it is a minor offense;

and when a lay bodhisattva, although it concerns their own person, commits an offense because it is contrary to reason, it is likewise a minor offense. 4. Those that are exclusively grave and not minor; this refers to what is properly established as this precept.
This is a heavy precept.

The fourth is the precept against false speech, also known as the precept of not speaking falsely. It is established for both the Great and Small Vehicles and is studied by all seven classes of followers.

The three sections are the same as in the preceding precepts. If one speaks of having attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) and thereby commits a great falsehood, it constitutes a primary offense of the heavy category. If it is a minor falsehood...

"Speech [of falsehood] is a minor offense; therefore, it is included here alongside what has been established. Regarding "lying oneself," there should be five propositions: First, in the case of a great lie where one perceives it as a lie—whether the magnitude is large or small—the offense is equally grave, because the object and the mental state correspond.

Second, in the case of a great lie where one suspects it is a minor lie, or a minor lie where one suspects it is a minor lie, there is no *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring formal meeting of the community), yet it is a grave offense.
If the mental state is divided, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave transgression); in the Mahāyāna, it is likewise grave. Third...
1. Perceiving a minor falsehood as a major falsehood: a third category offense (*tṛtīya-varga*) in the Hīnayāna; a minor offense in the Mahāyāna. 2. Perceiving a major falsehood as a minor falsehood:
a third category offense in the Hīnayāna; a minor offense in the Mahāyāna. 3. Doubting whether a minor falsehood is a major falsehood: a third category offense in the Hīnayāna;
a minor offense in the Mahāyāna. 4. Teaching another to speak falsely: a third category offense in the Hīnayāna.
This is because one anticipates personal gain. If one tells you a lie for one's own sake, it is invariably grave.
If one does not anticipate personal gain but tells you a lie, then teaching a great bhikṣu to lie constitutes a grave offense;

teaching a śrāmaṇera or those of lower rank to lie belongs to the third category [of offenses]. If it concerns a follower of the Mahāyāna, whether for your sake or for my own, it is invariably grave. Thus it is said.

Regarding "uttering false speech": although one does not verbally utter a great falsehood, one manifests various deeds so that others understand them to mean, "I have attained the Dharma of the Noble Ones.
Thus, it is said that this exists for the sake of obtaining fame and profit; this is called "false speech by means of expedient devices. As stated in the Vinaya:
"The nāgas come, the devas come, and they make offerings to us. The origin story (nidāna) is explained in detail in the Vinaya; this is an illustration thereof.

Regarding the term "hill" (kū): at the moment of making a great false speech, one commits the grave offense of lying; subsequently, upon obtaining the object, one commits the grave offense of preparatory theft.

Among the full set of conditions, seven factors must be complete for the offense to be grave: first, [the distinction between] addressing a human being versus addressing a non-human being and so forth, because [the latter] constitutes a light offense;
second, perceiving a human being as a non-human being, because this constitutes a light offense; third, knowing for oneself...

To have the perception that one has attained what has not been attained is also a secondary offense because it involves arrogance. Fourth, to give rise to a deluded and deceptive mind; if the mind is confused from beginning to end, there is no fault at all.
Fifth, to claim to have attained human or dharmic qualities. Sixth, to speak of karma with complete clarity. Seventh, when another person has already understood.
Among these, the first two and the seventh constitute the conditions (*pratyaya*), while the third constitutes the dharma (*dharma*). As for the fourth...

The causes are the fifth and sixth [factors], which constitute the karma. If the causes are entirely absent, there is no offense; yet if the conditions are absent, there is likewise no offense, nor is there even a minor offense.
The phrase "up to" (*yāvat*) refers to everything from great false speech down to minor false speech; hence the term "up to.

Regarding "saying one has seen what was not seen," among the categories of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, we take "seeing" as the primary example. The eight types of minor false speech constitute minor offenses. It is also thus.
Idle chatter, double-tongued speech, and harsh words all incur minor offenses. Furthermore, one incurs an offense when the body and mouth act in mutual opposition.

For example, when a donor builds a monastery and says, "Only those who have attained Arhatship may enter my monastery; otherwise, do not enter," if at that time he does not attain Arhatship but nevertheless enters and departs, [he incurs an offense].
Again, if he asks, "Have you attained the Noble Dharma? and at that time he manifests his head and body [to deceive], [he incurs an offense].

Because it constitutes a transgression, the grave offense of a great lie (*mahāmṛṣāvāda*) is incurred. Regarding the phrase "correct speech" (*samyag-vāk*), this refers to the eight kinds of correct language (*aṣṭavidha-samyag-vāk*).

Regarding "right view" (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*), according to the general interpretation, this refers to the three roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*), namely non-greed and so forth. These may also be analyzed through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*): first, that which is merit alone and not demerit;
this refers to cases such as a Bodhisattva who has attained mastery using false speech to deliver sentient beings. Second, that which is neither demerit nor merit.

That is to say, it refers to speaking while in a state of mental derangement, and so forth. Third, there are cases that are minor and not grave, referring to the minor false speech and other offenses established alongside this precept.
Fourth, there are cases that are grave and not minor, referring specifically to the major false speech formally established within this precept.
Regarding these four aforementioned precepts, both the Great and Small Vehicles study them together; they are collectively proscribed for all seven classes of practitioners.
The fifth precept concerns the sale of intoxicants, also known as the precept against selling intoxicants. This regulation applies equally to both the Great and Small Vehicles;

in the Small Vehicle, it is categorized as a violation of the third grade for the two higher assemblies (monks and nuns), while for the three lower assemblies (novices, probationers, and female probationers), it is a violation of the fifth grade.

In the Mahāyāna, the sale of intoxicants is considered a grave offense for all seven assemblies. If one sells items such as the *śīrṣaka* (a type of weapon) or other implements used for killing, it constitutes a minor defilement. If, as [the text continues]:

Regarding the selling of religious objects: for a lay bodhisattva, it is not prohibited as long as they have not yet abandoned their livelihood-generating activities. Thus, the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states:
"One may sell one portion of the goods obtained. Regarding the measure of alcohol: according to the Hīnayāna, if it is one-fourth [of the standard measure], it constitutes an offense.

The limit is defined by that which can intoxicate a person. According to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, if one produces alcohol, it constitutes a transgression of the limit whether it intoxicates or not.
According to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-sūtra*, there are three types: grain liquor, medicinal liquor, and herb liquor. Herb liquor refers to things such as grape wine that intoxicates people;
medicinal liquor refers to those made from herbs such as *duhuo* (dudhura) and so forth. These are called "true" [alcohols].
Regarding alcohol as the condition for the arising of various transgressions, this is explained according to the precept against drinking intoxicants.
As for the term "all kinds of alcohol," it includes substances that resemble alcohol, namely sweet wine, fermented dregs, and similar varieties. Zhong says:

"Sweet, sour, and dreg-based grain wines" refers to wheat flour soaked in wine and dried, which is capable of causing intoxication. Within the category of selling alcohol, there are five propositions; the first is the actual [act].
First, if one perceives actual alcohol as actual alcohol, one commits a grave offense. Second, if one perceives actual alcohol with doubt regarding its nature, it is likewise grave.

Third, if one perceives actual alcohol as not being actual alcohol, if one subsequently shifts that perception, one commits a light offense; however, if one initially mistakes the object for something other than alcohol, there is no offense at all.

If one gives rise to delusion regarding an object that resembles alcohol, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). (4) Regarding what is not alcohol, if one perceives it as true alcohol, it is a minor offense.

(5) Regarding what is not true alcohol, if one suspects it is true alcohol, it is a minor offense. To teach others within the Mahāyāna—whether saying "it is for me" or "it is for you"—is grave in both cases.

In the Hīnayāna, both are offenses concerning the precept against selling [alcohol]. Regarding the completion of the conditions: seven conditions constitute a grave offense. The first is when the person to whom it is given is a non-human (*amanuṣya*).
Because it is light [in nature]. Second, because one perceives two people as non-humans and thus treats them lightly. Third, because true alcohol and alcohol-like substances are light [in nature].
Fourth, because there is no offense for one who forms the perception of selling alcohol but does not harbor the intention to sell it.

Fifth, giving it to that person. Sixth, receiving the price. Seventh, that person drinking it. Among these, the first two and the seventh constitute one condition; the fourth constitutes one [condition].
The causes: the third and first are the dharmas; the fifth and sixth are the karma. Regarding "clear penetration" (*vidyā*): to illuminate principle is "clarity" (*vidyā*);

to know phenomena is "penetration" (*pratisaṃvit*). This is also a term for the gates. One interpretation states that taking the three types of penetration as "penetration" also yields four propositions:

first, merit alone and not demerit—this refers to Bodhisattvas who penetrate the capacities [of beings]; second, neither demerit nor merit—this refers to making wine for medicinal purposes and giving it to others.
First, because it involves taking payment, it is not merit; because it is medicinal wine, it is not a transgression. Third, it is merely light and not heavy;

this is established as being similar to [the prohibition of] alcohol and the like within the category of "I" (self). Fourth, it is exclusively sexual misconduct and not light; this is what is correctly established as the selling of actual wine and so forth within this precept.
The sixth section concerns the precept on accusing a fellow practitioner of a fault; there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

In the Hīnayāna, because self-benefit is prioritized, accusing someone of a grave offense without basis is classified as a second-category offense (*dvitīya-āpatti*). This is because the mental transgression of slandering another with false matters is considered a heavy fault.

Conversely, if one accuses another of a fault based on a valid ground (*sāpattika*), it is a fault of intention, as the accusation is made by citing a factual matter. Thus, it is a mental transgression.

Because it is light, it constitutes an offense of the third category. For one who follows the Mahāyāna, since the priority is benefiting others, if one slanders another by stating a fact, the other’s matter is successfully undermined;
because the harm to the welfare of others is grave, this is established as a heavy precept due to its having a basis (*sāpadeśa*).
If, however, one slanders without a basis, although it may incidentally affect others, the other’s matter is not successfully undermined; thus, the harm to others...
The meaning is that it is a minor transgression; therefore, it is designated as the thirteenth light impurity offense (*āpatti*).

If one belonging to the Hīnayāna school slanders another with a groundless grave offense, they commit an offense of the second category. If one slanders another by citing a grounded grave offense or a groundless offense of the second category, they commit an offense of the third category.
Within the middle section, there are three parts: first, identifying the person to indicate the essence [of the offense]; second, enumerating the matters to clarify the principle; third...
This raises the fault of being unwholesome. Within this, there are two parts: first, the formal enumeration of the faults; second, the demonstration of the remedial correct practice.

Within the first part, there are also two: first, the formal enumeration of the faults; second, the clarification of how the action is completed through the presence of its constituent conditions. Regarding the specific identification of the person being slandered:

Regarding the grave offenses of the fourfold assembly who have received the Bodhisattva precepts: this refers to slandering ordained monks (*bhikṣu*) and nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), as well as the two lay assemblies, by falsely accusing them of having committed the ten root transgressions, the seven heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), or other such faults. If one actually commits such a grave violation of the precepts, it constitutes a grave offense.

If one slanders them by raising a minor offense, one commits a minor offense. If one slanders those who are *śrāvakas*, it constitutes a grave offense if one raises a fundamental offense from the first category (*āpatti-prathama*) of either of the two aforementioned assemblies.

Those who commit this grave precept together—whether they raise the minor offenses of the two higher assemblies, or the major and minor offenses of the lower assembly that possess roots—all such slanderers commit an offense;

furthermore, a light defilement offense (*āpatti*) is established. Within the section on "speaking for oneself," there are five points: first, regarding a grave offense with the perception of it being a grave offense, one commits a grave offense;
second, regarding a grave offense with doubt as to whether it is a grave offense, one commits a grave offense; third, regarding a grave offense that is not actually a grave offense...

Regarding perception (*saṃjñā*): if one perceives [the act] as a transgression while it is actually a transformation of perception, one commits a minor offense (*laghu-pāpaka*). If one is fundamentally deluded [as to the nature of the object], it exceeds the scope of the prohibited domain and there is no offense at all.

If one exceeds the scope of a minor offense while being deluded, one commits a minor offense. Fourth, if one perceives what is not a grave offense (*sthūla-tyaya*) as a grave offense, one commits a minor offense.
Fifth, if one has doubt regarding whether an offense is grave, one commits a minor offense. Regarding instructing others to speak of transgressions: [instructing them to speak of] a grave offense...

If he slanders another on my behalf, or slanders another on your behalf, he commits a grave offense in all cases. Eight conditions must be fulfilled for it to constitute a grave offense: first, the parties involved share the same precepts and the same Dharma;

second, the slander is directed toward those of the two higher groups among the seven classes of practitioners; third, the slanderer intends to malign those outside the [Buddhist] fold or those of the three lower groups who share the same precepts and the same Dharma—because if these conditions are not met, the offense is minor;
fourth, there is the perception that they share the same precepts and the same Dharma; fifth, there is a mind defiled by anger; and so forth. If...
Regarding those who speak without a mind of transgression: because they commit a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). Fourth, the intention involves a false perception.
Fifth, the seven heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten grave offenses constitute a heavy transgression; whereas if one slanders [another] regarding a minor offense, it constitutes a minor offense.

Sixth, whether speaking to a human or speaking to a non-human (*amanuṣya*), it is a minor offense. Seventh, the words must be clear. Eighth, the person addressed must understand them. The first two [points]...
Furthermore, the fourth and sixth [factors] together with four others serve as conditions; the third serves as the cause; the fifth serves as the phenomenon (*dharma*);

and the latter two serve as the activity (*karman*). Because non-Buddhists and wicked people regard the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) as *nirvāṇa*, they mistake what is not supreme for the supreme.
Moreover, because they observe practices such as the "cow-vow" which are not the true path, their evil views increase regarding themselves and others. Consequently, they fall into the evil realms.
Because they head toward [lower realms], they are called "evil persons. Regarding those who are evil persons among the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*):

the Tathāgata, relying on the gate of "not non-existent," spoke of them as existing for the sake of [those to be converted], stating that due to false attachment, they conceive of themselves as having fallen into evil states.

Because of this view, according to Mahāyāna scriptures, they cause both themselves and others to fall into the evil destinies (*durgati*); therefore, they are called evil persons. This refers to those who do not merely cling to the Lesser Vehicle as real, but who slander the Mahāyāna.

They are not called "evil persons" or "those who act contrary to the Dharma. If non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) take what is not supreme to be supreme, or if those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyānika*) take what is not the ultimate teaching to be the ultimate—thereby contradicting the Mahāyāna *sūtras*—they are not called "mediators" (*madhyama*), because they do not manifest the departure from extremes.
Regarding the ten kinds of non-mediatory matters of the Vātsīputrīyas and others, there are likewise four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First: merit alone, not transgression.

First, those that contravene the faculties [of sentient beings]. Second, those that are neither merit nor transgression, such as the teachings given by one with a deranged mind. Third, those that are exclusively light and not grave;

this refers to cases where the precepts established here include instances that, when cited, result in accusations of having committed only minor offenses. Fourth, those that are exclusively grave and not light;
these refer to the grave precepts established within this very category of precepts.
The seventh precept concerns praising oneself and disparaging others; it is also called the precept of praising oneself and disparaging others for the sake of gain.

This precept is established as a common rule for all seven classes of practitioners and is studied by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna followers. The details are the same as the preceding precepts; herein, five points clarify the underlying intent:

first, if one does not seek gain but merely praises oneself and disparages others, one commits only a light offense. Second, if one does not seek gain but merely disparages others and does not praise oneself, one commits only a light offense.

Third, hoping for a benefit of five *kārsāpaṇas* or less while praising oneself and disparaging others: this constitutes a light offense. Fourth, hoping for a benefit of more than five *kārsāpaṇas* while praising oneself and disparaging others:

this constitutes a formal violation of this precept. Fifth, having resolved to hope for a benefit of more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, with a mind that elevates what is heavy and exceeds the limit, while praising oneself and disparaging others:
this constitutes two grave offenses, namely this precept and the preceding one. Question: What if one does not hope for a benefit?
Question: Why does it involve both praising oneself and disparaging others? Answer: It constitutes only a minor offense (light defilement). Question:

Although one may hope for a profit exceeding five coins while praising oneself and disparaging others, why is it that [the offense] is absent when either is missing? Answer: It should be considered grave. Question:

How is it known that this precept is violated only when one hopes for a profit exceeding five coins? Answer: The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-śāstra* (or *Dharmadhātu-vibhaṅga-śāstra*) states: "Regarding the hope for profit..."
If one praises oneself and disparages others out of self-interest, one commits a multitude of offenses. It is understood that for those with five *kārsāpaṇas* or fewer, the offense is light;

only when it exceeds five *kārsāpaṇas* does it become a grave offense. If one has the intention to obtain five *kārsāpaṇas* or more while praising oneself and disparaging others—regardless of whether the money is actually obtained—is this a grave precept?
According to Master Run, one commits this grave offense only upon obtaining the five *kārsāpaṇas*. If [the money] is obtained...
Regarding "money," it is a grave matter; violating this precept and the precept against stealing are both grave offenses.
As for self-praise and disparaging others, there are six types mentioned in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*: first, being born into a low-caste family; second, having a lowly occupation;
third, having lowly skills or craftsmanship; fourth, saying, "You are one who has committed transgressions"; fifth, saying, "You have done much [evil]... [and so forth].
Regarding the fetters and compulsions: the sixth [type of person] refers to those who are blind or bald and sightless.

Among the forms of self-praise, these six types of praise—where one says of oneself, "I am superior to them"—should be understood. Within these six categories, according to the Hīnayāna, all constitute the third category of offense.
In the Mahāyāna, among these six, if one praises oneself and disparages others out of greed, it constitutes a direct violation of this grave precept. Within this, there is further differentiation.
Regarding the fourth point, exposing faults: if one exposes a grave fault based on grounds, one commits two grave offenses—namely, the preceding precept and this present precept.
If one does not seek personal gain and exposes a grave fault based on grounds, one commits the preceding precept but does not commit this present precept.
If one exposes a grave fault without grounds, a light fault with grounds, or any of the other five types of faults, these all constitute minor secondary offenses (light defilements).

It is not a grave offense. Furthermore, if one uses wholesome dharmas—such as merely scolding you for practicing *araṇya* (solitude), up to practicing meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth—in the Small Vehicle, it is a minor offense;

in the Mahāyāna, it is a light defilement (*laghu-āpatti*) provided no profit is sought. Teaching others to praise or slander [the practitioner] constitutes an equal grave offense. When six conditions are fully met, a grave offense is established:
first, as before, it concerns the seven classes of practitioners who share the same Dharma, specifically the two higher classes; second, the analogy must concern a person who shares the same Dharma.
1. Perception (*saṃjñā*). 2. The three common pure benefits (*śuddhārtha*). 3. Speaking of oneself by way of analogy. 4. Clarity of expression. 5.

The listener’s understanding and comprehension. Among these, the first two constitute the conditions (*pratyaya*); the third constitutes the cause (*hetu*); the fourth constitutes the dharma (*dharma*);

and the latter two constitute the function (*karma*). These should be formulated as five propositions: first, by virtue of a compassionate mind, for the sake of causing that person to give rise to faith and the bodhicitta, one [speaks] oneself...
1. To praise oneself and disparage others with a mind that is entirely free of fault is neutral (*avyākṛta*).

Since these two types of students are foolish and coarse in speech, praising oneself and disparaging others while in such a neutral state of mind constitutes a minor offense; this is called an "unafflicted transgression" (*akliṣṭāpatti*). 2.

To praise oneself and disparage others out of a sense of equality, due to constant concealment, or because of harboring resentment toward that person, also constitutes a minor offense of defilement; this is called an "afflicted transgression" (*kliṣṭāpatti*).
There are four [conditions] for an offense: fourth, because of praising oneself and disparaging others for the sake of a profit of five *kārsāpaṇas* or more;
fifth, because of being deranged or having a distracted mind. One who praises oneself and disparages others under these conditions commits no offense at all. The text states:

"Regarding the five phrases concerning directing evil toward oneself and giving good to others, one does not consider the first phrase; one considers only the latter four phrases. Therefore, this statement was made.
There are also four propositions. First, exclusively merit and not demerit; this refers to bodhisattvas who have attained the capacity [for realization] and those who study erroneously.
Regarding the first of the five preceding propositions, the first case is due to a virtuous mind, whereby one praises or disparages slightly. Second, neither merit nor demerit;
this refers to categories such as those with distracted minds. Third, only light and not heavy; this refers to gains of five coins or less. [One] praises...

Regarding the category of disparaging and so forth: four [offenses] are grave only and not light. This precept is formally established in relation to benefits exceeding five coins; it concerns praising and disparaging and so forth.

The eighth is the precept against stinginess and adding disparagement. This precept is regulated for all seven classes of followers; while there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna regarding the training, the substance is the same.
Regarding the preceding section on stinginess (*mātsarya*), there are five propositions: 1. A poor person perceives another as poor; this constitutes a grave offense (*pārājika*). 2.

A poor person suspects another who is rich to be poor; this constitutes a grave offense. 3. A poor person perceives another who is rich to be poor. If this is analyzed according to a "shifted perception" (*parivṛtta-saṃjñā*), it is a light defilement offense (*duṣkṛta*) based on the prior intention.
If, however, it is a fundamental delusion (*mūla-moha*), and the delusion persists from beginning to end such that only the rich person is deluded, then there is no offense at all.
"Fourth, if one is wealthy but holds a poor person in contempt, it is a minor offense. Fifth, if one is wealthy but harbors suspicion toward a poor person, it is likewise a minor offense.

Regarding teaching others to be stingy for one's own sake or for their own sake, both constitute grave offenses. As for the requisite conditions: six conditions must be fulfilled for it to constitute a grave offense.

First, there is a sentient being who is impoverished and suffering. Second, the perception that they are impoverished and suffering. Third, one possesses wealth and treasures of one's own. Fourth, the mind of stinginess and attachment. If...
There is no such mind, because there is no offense whatsoever. Fifth, not giving wealth or Dharma, even as much as a single coin or a single phrase.
