Sixth, disparagement. Among these, the first two serve as conditions (*pratyaya*); the third serves as the object (*dharma*); the fourth serves as the cause (*hetu*);

and the fifth and sixth serve as the action (*karman*). Regarding "even a single atom of Dharma": it refers to the smallest atom within the smallest particle of form (*rūpa*) contained in a single phrase.
The smallest among forms serves as an analogy for the smallest among dharmas. There are also four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1. Stinginess and giving:
this is exclusively merit (*puṇya*) and not demerit (*apuṇya*). This refers to the Bodhisattva who has attained mastery over capacities. 2. Neither demerit nor merit:

this refers to those who have been consistently wealthy throughout their fundamental delusion. Because they do not give, it is not merit; because they are wealthy, it is not demerit. 3. Only light and not heavy: this refers to...
Regarding the first five phrases: within the first part of the third phrase, it is explained by way of a poor person.

Even when one perceives a wealthy person and so forth as being in a wealthy state, yet forms the perception of them as poor, or harbors doubt regarding them, this constitutes the fourth [category]: that which is grave and not light;
this is precisely what is established here as a grave offense within this precept.

The ninth precept concerns anger, striking, and harboring resentment; it is also called the precept against being angry and refusing to accept an apology. It is prescribed for all seven classes of followers, though there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions.

The structure of the offense is the same as in the preceding precepts. Regarding the first part—anger itself—one should formulate five propositions: first, committing a grave offense by reacting irrationally to an object of one's own anger;
second, committing a grave offense when the object is not irrational but one suspects it is; third, [committing a grave offense when] the object is irrational... [and so forth].

If one harbors such thoughts, or if those thoughts change, one commits a minor offense (*āpatti*). If one was originally deluded, one likewise commits a minor offense. Fourth, when there is a principle that is not a principle;
fifth, when there is doubt regarding what is a principle or not a principle—both constitute the commission of a minor defiling offense (*laghu-mala-āpatti*).

Why is this so? Because for a Bodhisattva to give rise to anger violates the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Within the instruction to cause others to feel anger, whether it be "I am angry" or "you are angry," both equally constitute a grave offense.

Furthermore, the full seven conditions constitute a grave offense. This is because if the person is non-human and one is angry, it is light. [The seven conditions are: first, the perception that it is a person; second, the arousal of anger; third, the utterance of harsh words;
fourth, striking with the hand or a staff; fifth, not accepting an apology; sixth, harboring resentment without relinquishing it; and seventh, the completion of the act.
Among these, the first two serve as the conditions (*pratyaya*); the third alone serves as the cause (*hetu*); and the fourth and fifth together serve as the factors (*dharma*). The latter...
The second [type] constitutes an offense. How is it known that harboring resentment and failing to relinquish it constitutes a grave offense? The *Śīlabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"If one utters harsh words, seizes wood or stones, or strikes and beats others with a staff, one commits numerous offenses.

Thus, we know that if one harbors resentment and does not relinquish it, it is merely a light defilement offense (*pāyattika*), not a grave one. Within these, seizing a staff is a bodily action, while uttering harsh words is a vocal action.

Therefore, it constitutes a grave offense only when [the conditions] are fully met. If one merely utters harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) while harboring anger and resentment without relinquishing them, yet does not employ physical actions such as wielding a staff or striking, it is merely light and not grave.

Alternatively, if one commits an improper act toward another person while harboring resentment and refusing to let go, it constitutes only a light offense and not a grave one. However, if one is able to treat the angry person improperly...
Regarding the person toward whom one feels anger who is upright and principled, the formation of heavy karma is also analyzed through four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): 1. Only merit and not demerit:
This refers to Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery over their faculties. 2. Neither merit nor demerit: This refers to those such as those with deranged minds. 3. Only light and not heavy:

This refers to the establishment within this precept of various forms of anger directed toward non-sentient beings and the like. 4. Only heavy and not light: This refers specifically to anger within the scope of this very precept.
This establishes the grave precepts.

The tenth is the precept against slandering the Triple Gem. It is prescribed for all seven assemblies of practitioners, though there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions. This is the same precept as mentioned previously;
because it involves slandering the Triple Gem, the matter is presented through specific instances. Briefly, there are four such cases. First, those who are icchantikas, due to their lack of...

First, because they obstruct faith, they slander the Triple Gem; the reason for this is easily understood. Second, those with the mind of an outsider (tīrthika) mistake what is not the Way for the Way and what is not the Dharma for the Dharma;
thus, they slander the Buddha-Dharma. Third, those of the Two Vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) take that which is not ultimate to be ultimate, and thus they slander the Mahāyāna scriptures.
An illustration of their characteristics is found in the *Jiujiao jing* (Scripture on the Nine Teachings), which states that they do not teach the Buddha-nature.
For these reasons, they do not understand the Buddha; that is to say, because they cling to the teaching of the Dharma, they fail to clarify the Buddha-nature and slander the Mahāyāna.

Because the sacred doctrine of the Buddha-nature clarifies this meaning, it can be understood through its exclusion. Fourth is the Mahāyāna, which possesses the two attachments to existence and emptiness.

To briefly cite an example to manifest its characteristics: here, in explaining the gate of "neither non-existence nor existence" regarding the person and the Buddha as conceived by the masters, we provisionally speak of all existences.

Therefore, as it is said, one should grasp the meaning. Thus, while they are clung to and conceived as substantially existent, they are also designated as non-existent based on their lack of existence.

Furthermore, if the Tathāgata is the true nature (*tattva*), he is non-existent according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); yet, when considering the Buddha’s intention, he is said to exist conventionally.
Because one does not apprehend the mark of non-existence, it is said to "exist"; yet this is not because one apprehends the mark of existence that it is said to exist.
Therefore, without moving from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one establishes all phenomena. Furthermore, the meaning of the Tathāgata’s teaching that all phenomena are empty is this:

because one does not apprehend the mark of existence, they are said to be "empty"; yet this is not because one apprehends the mark of emptiness that they are called "empty. Therefore, one does not destroy conventional designations.
To speak of the true nature (*dharmatā*) by means of names, those people have not yet understood such a Middle Way that is free from existence and non-existence.

Therefore, when they enter into reality, they immediately reject and uproot cause and effect; thus, they destroy conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Because they claim to speak of the true nature only after destroying these designations, they incur the fault of damaging the cognition of grasping (*grāhaka-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, because they emerge from conventional truth while clinging to it as being truly existent, they disturb the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is because they attempt to establish all phenomena only after having disturbed that limit. Thus...
They form an adherence to superimposition. Yet, while adhering to such similar calculations, they slander the Buddha’s vast Dharma-gate, saying, "This is right and that is wrong.

Because they judge from the perspective of the thoroughly imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) in relation to the Tathāgata who is definitively free from extremes, this emptiness contradicts the Buddha as much as heaven contradicts earth.
Nevertheless, they adhere to the claim, "My intention accords with the Tathāgata’s intention," and thus they slander him.
Regarding the Jewel of the Buddha: because various conceptualizations hold that what is non-existent should not be considered as such, they claim it exists.
Yet, this conceptualization of existence and the conceptualization of non-existence are not identical to the One Suchness (tathatā). Therefore, it transcends words and is beyond thought.

To conceptually construct and then slanderously claim that it is real—saying, "It is as I have taught"—is to slander the Jewel of the Dharma and to slander the person who can teach it, asserting, "What I have said is true, for what that person has said is false."
Because one slanders the conduct of the Saṃgha, a single statement simultaneously constitutes a slander of the Triple Gem; therefore, one commits a grave offense (pārājika).

That this constitutes a grave offense is known from the *Śrīkṣitigarbha-sūtra-śāstra*, which states: "To slander the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and establish counterfeit teachings—whether for oneself or for the sake of the Saṃgha—is to slander the True Dharma by establishing counterfeit teachings; thus one commits a grave offense. Therefore, it is known that this constitutes a grave offense.

Teaching others to slander the Triple Gem constitutes an equal offense of gravity. Four conditions must be fulfilled for the grave karma to be completed: first, there is a false understanding; second, one gives rise to the intentional resolve to slander;
third, one slanders before a person—if one slanders before a non-human being and so forth, one commits a minor offense (light垢罪);

fourth, the person before whom one speaks understands as described above. However, the Dharma Master says that it is only when one explains a false doctrine and establishes it as complete that the offense is fully constituted.
This is grave. If one slanders [the Dharma] or expounds false teachings, yet does not establish the full penetration, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).

Therefore, regarding those who slander the true Dharma, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-śāstra* (or *Dharmadhātu-vibhaṅga*) states that if one expounds false teachings without establishing the full penetration, it is considered light.

The Dharma Master said: Regarding those who possess the full complement of conditions, seven conditions constitute a grave offense: first, having internal wrong views; second, the person toward whom one directs oneself;

third, the perception that the person is human; fourth, preaching false dharma; fifth, establishing the completion of the communication; sixth, the words being clearly articulated; and seventh, [the listener] understanding the meaning.

The seven preceding points are understood as follows: among them, the first constitutes the cause (*hetu*); the second and third constitute the conditions (*pratyaya*); the fourth and fifth constitute the dharma; and the final two constitute the activity (*karma*).
Regarding the "master" (*ācārya*) mentioned [in the commentary]: this refers not to one who slanders the Triple Gem, but rather to those such as non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
However, this does not accord with the meaning. Why? Because this precept concerns the teacher of one who has received the Buddha’s precepts; it does not apply to one who slanders [the Triple Gem].
This is because of the Three Jewels. It is because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others do not receive the Bodhisattva precepts. One should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

First: that which is merit alone and not transgression. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The ten types of sages and non-Buddhists, having attained the capacity [of a Bodhisattva], manifest among non-Buddhists as high-ranking leaders.
Later, when debating with the Buddha, they manifest the appearance of being defeated. Leading the assembly of non-Buddhists, they enter..."
First, those similar to the Buddha-dharma; second, those that are neither sinful nor meritorious, such as states of deranged mind;

third, those that are only light and not grave, namely, slandering the true Dharma while failing to establish the Dharma and so forth, or slandering the true Dharma toward non-humans and establishing counterfeit dharmas and the like;
fourth, those that are only grave and not light, namely, the grave precepts properly established within this code of discipline.
Among these ten grave precepts, if they are ranked by way of the paths of karma (*karmapatha*), taking life is the gravest, because its meaning of harming others is extremely serious.
If they are ranked by the breadth of the transgression, lying is the gravest, as it involves slandering the sages.
Because I have become such a noble one, the realms toward which I direct myself eternally encompass all ordinary and saintly persons throughout the ten directions.

If one considers that which is most grievous to be "heavy," then the precept against sexual misconduct is the heaviest, as it is the fundamental source for giving rise to the karmic offenses of the Dharma. Thus, among the ten heavy precepts, three are explained here;
first, the general explanation and exhortation to study has been provided, and second, the detailed explanation of the prohibitions has already been concluded previously.
Below this is the third section, the summary of the re-enactment of the precepts. This contains three parts: first, the explanation of the re-enactment as an exhortation to study;
second, from "If there should be one who transgresses" onwards, the explanation of the re-enactment as an exhortation to observe the conditions; and third, the summary of the exhortation to study.
The beginning and middle also have two parts. First, it clarifies the persons being exhorted; second, it expresses the Dharma being exhorted. Regarding the initial phrase "those who learn well":

because Bodhisattvas possess the virtue of ethical discipline within, and are externally able to provide understanding to all people—being entirely without fault and entirely correct—they are called "those who learn well. Since such persons are not singular, the term "all people" is used. Thus it is said:
One should not commit even so much as a single speck of dust of such offenses, let alone committing them in their entirety. Regarding the violation of the ten precepts, there are two explanations.
First, it is said that one must not commit even a speck of dust of the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) for an offense, let alone committing them in full.
As for each and every one of these grave karmas, they must not be committed even toward a single precept, let alone committing all ten precepts.

The second section, "Indicating the States," also has two parts: first, clarifying the loss of status; second, clarifying the experience of suffering. Within the first part, there are two sub-sections:
first, clarifying the loss of worldly status; second, indicating the supramundane status. Regarding the term "king," this refers to a king among humans, namely a minor king (*kṣudra-rāja*).
As for the status of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) according to a specific classification, the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) constitutes the Iron [Wheel-Turning] King.

Regarding the Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*): one who has attained the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) is a copper-wheel-turning king; one who has attained the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) is a silver-wheel-turning king;

and one who has attained the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) is a gold-wheel-turning king. If categorized according to the general gate, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is a hundred-jewel wheel-turning king, and the second stage is a thousand-jewel wheel-turning king.

Within this gate, both those prior to the stages (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*) and those within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are all wheel-turning kings, as explained at length in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Ratnarāśi-sūtra*).
"Losing the royal throne" clarifies the loss of the status of a householder. "Losing the status of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī" clarifies the loss of the status of one who has left the household life.
Regarding the second section, which clarifies the experience of suffering, the mention of "two or three kalpas" is as follows:

according to the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Ābharaṇa-sūtra*), those who have committed grave offenses enter hell for ten kalpas. The commentary explains that this sūtra refers to *antarakalpas* (minor kalpas). Thus it is said.
It is for ten *kalpas*. In this text, the mention of two or three *kalpas* refers to *mahākalpas*. That sutra states:
"Those who commit grave offenses and fall into hell undergo eighty-four thousand births and deaths within a single day.
Regarding what is explained in the eighty-thousand-verse section on the *Āyatanas*, it is, for example, as described in the twenty-odd fascicles of the Hīnayāna Vinaya concerning monks and nuns.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* first provides a general teaching on the precepts and subsequently offers a definitive exposition; this sūtra is likewise.

Furthermore, within the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the ten grave prohibitions are first stated in summary, and they are later explained in greater detail within the "Chapter on the Eighty Thousand Modes of Conduct.
Therefore, these are the locations where the texts are presented.
In the twelfth month of the forty-third year of the Meiji era, the editor-in-chief of the *Zokuzōkyō*, Master Nakano Tatsu-e, stated:
"This book is a rare work not preserved in other collections; we request that you transcribe it so that it may be included in the *Zokuzōkyō*.
I promptly responded to this request, granted permission for the transcription, and recorded its details.
The facts are hereby presented.
On an auspicious day in the first month of the forty-fourth year of Meiji, the forty-fourth generation of the Dharma-lamp, the śramaṇa Seijō, proclaims this throughout the four seas. On this day.
